children.title: Scalar Multiplication Limits
children.top_down_role: Limiting behavior under varying scalar multiplication.

assumptions_latex: \(A_n,A\) are nonempty compact subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^d\) contained in one compact set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_nA_n\to\lambda A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar-set multiplication with uniform boundedness, including zero limiting scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A_n,A\) be nonempty compact subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^d\), contained in a common compact set, and suppose \(A_n\to A\). If \(\lambda_n\to\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\), then
\[
\lambda_nA_n\to\lambda A,
\qquad
\lambda A=\{\lambda a:a\in A\}.
\]
Uniform boundedness controls the products when \(\lambda=0\); in particular, every sequence \(\lambda_na_n\) with \(a_n\in A_n\) converges to zero whenever \(\lambda_n\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convergent scalar factors preserve set convergence for compact sets sharing a common bound, including when the limiting scalar is zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Multiplication Limits

children.title: Degenerate Scaling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Scaling behavior near zero, infinity, or sign changes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_n\to\varnothing\) and \(\lambda_n\to0\), but \(\lambda_nA_n=\{1\}\to\{1\}\neq0\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of scaling continuity at zero when the sets escape to infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In \(\mathbb{R}\), take \(A_n=\{n\}\) and \(\lambda_n=1/n\). The sets escape every bounded region, hence \(A_n\to\varnothing\) in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense, while \(\lambda_n\to0\). Nevertheless,
\[
\lambda_nA_n=\{1\}\to\{1\}.
\]
Thus the formal limiting expression \(0\varnothing=\varnothing\) does not describe the scaled-set limit. At a zero limiting scale, boundedness or an equivalent control of \(\lambda_nA_n\) is indispensable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When sets escape at the reciprocal rate of a vanishing scalar, their scaled images can retain nonzero points despite an empty set limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Scaling Regimes

children.title: Minkowski Cancellation Failure
children.top_down_role: Loss of recoverability under Minkowski combination.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A+C=B+C=\{0,1,2,3\}\) although \(A\neq B\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-set counterexample to cancellation for Minkowski addition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
A=\{0,2\},\qquad B=\{0,1,2\},\qquad C=\{0,1\}
\]
in \(\mathbb{R}\). Direct calculation gives
\[
A+C=\{0,1,2,3\}=B+C,
\]
although \(A\neq B\). Hence Minkowski addition by a fixed nonempty compact set is not injective on arbitrary compact sets, and equality or convergence of sums cannot generally be canceled to recover equality or convergence of the summands.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minkowski addition is not cancellative: distinct finite sets can have identical sums with the same compact set.
knowledge_statements.title: Minkowski Cancellation Failure
Images Under Varying Mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniformly convergent mappings acting on uniformly compact set sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^p\) be compact, and let \(A_n,A\subset K\) be nonempty compact sets with \(A_n\to A\). Suppose continuous mappings \(f_n,f:K\to\mathbb{R}^q\) satisfy
\[
\sup_{x\in K}\|f_n(x)-f(x)\|\to0.
\]
Then
\[
f_n(A_n)\to f(A).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform convergence of mappings and compact convergence of their domains imply convergence of the corresponding image sets.
assumptions_latex: \(A_n,A\) are nonempty compact subsets of a common compact set \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^p\), with \(A_n\to A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n(A_n)\to f(A)\).

notation.meaning: image of a set under a mapping

children.title: Inverse-Image Limits
children.top_down_role: Convergence behavior of inverse images under varying mappings or target sets.

assumptions_latex: \(f_n,f:\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R}^q\) are continuous and \(f_n\to f\) locally uniformly; closed sets \(D_n\to D\).
For every \(z\in f^{-1}(D)\), locally and eventually \(d(x,f_n^{-1}(D_n))\leq\kappa d(f_n(x),D_n)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inverse-image convergence under local uniform mapping convergence and metric regularity.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Sequential Normal Compactness of Set Intersections and Inverse Images p. 341
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let continuous mappings \(f_n,f:\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R}^q\) satisfy \(f_n\to f\) locally uniformly, and let closed sets \(D_n\to D\). Put \(F_n=f_n^{-1}(D_n)\) and \(F=f^{-1}(D)\). Suppose that for every \(z\in F\) there exist a neighborhood \(U\), \(\kappa>0\), and \(n_0\) such that
\[
d(x,F_n)\leq\kappa d(f_n(x),D_n)
\]
for \(x\in U\) and \(n\geq n_0\). Then \(F_n\to F\) in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inverse images converge when mappings and target sets converge and a uniform local error bound supplies feasible recovery points.
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Image Limits

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Sequential Normal Compactness of Set Intersections and Inverse Images p. 341
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Feasible-Set Convergence
children.top_down_role: Set limits arising from parameterized feasibility systems.

assumptions_latex: For every \(z\in F=\{g\leq0\}\), locally and eventually \(d(x,F_n)\leq\kappa\|[g_n(x)]_+\|\), where \(F_n=\{g_n\leq0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_n\to F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence of finite inequality systems under a uniform residual error bound.

source_refs.locator: 4.3.2 Lipschitzian Stability of Constraint Systems p. 414
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let continuous mappings \(g_n,g:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfy \(g_n\to g\) locally uniformly, and define
\[
F_n=\{x:g_n(x)\leq0\},\qquad F=\{x:g(x)\leq0\},
\]
with componentwise inequalities. Suppose that for every \(z\in F\) there exist a neighborhood \(U\), \(\kappa>0\), and \(n_0\) such that
\[
d(x,F_n)\leq\kappa\|[g_n(x)]_+\|
\]
for \(x\in U\) and \(n\geq n_0\). Then \(F_n\to F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible sets of convergent inequality systems converge when constraint violation uniformly controls distance to feasibility near every limiting feasible point.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Set Convergence

source_witnesses.locator: 4.3.2 Lipschitzian Stability of Constraint Systems p. 414
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Inverse-Image Regularity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regularity limits governing preservation of inverse-image convergence.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_n\xrightarrow{PK}D\), but \(f^{-1}(D_n)\not\xrightarrow{PK}f^{-1}(D)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of inverse-image continuity when the limiting target value is attained but the approximating values lie outside the mapping range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Inverse images need not preserve Painlevé–Kuratowski convergence. For the stated sets, \(D_n\xrightarrow{PK}D\), while \(f^{-1}(D_n)=\varnothing\) for every \(n\in\mathbb N\) and \(f^{-1}(D)=\{0\}\). Hence \(f^{-1}(D_n)\not\xrightarrow{PK}f^{-1}(D)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convergent target sets can have nonconvergent inverse images when their limit is attained but all approximating values lie outside the mapping range.
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Image Regularity Boundary

children.title: Closure Stability
children.top_down_role: Interaction of closure with set convergence.

assumptions_latex: \((C_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\) is a sequence of subsets of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}\overline{C_n}=\liminf_{n\to\infty}C_n\) and \(\limsup_{n\to\infty}\overline{C_n}=\limsup_{n\to\infty}C_n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential Painlevé–Kuratowski limits in a metric space are unchanged by termwise closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Termwise closure leaves both sequential set limits unchanged:
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\overline{C_n}=\liminf_{n\to\infty}C_n,
\qquad
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\overline{C_n}=\limsup_{n\to\infty}C_n.
\]
Consequently, \(C_n\xrightarrow{PK}C\) implies \(\overline{C_n}\xrightarrow{PK}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking the closure of every set in a sequence leaves its inner and outer Painlevé–Kuratowski limits unchanged.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure Stability

children.title: Convexification Stability
children.top_down_role: Interaction of convex hull formation with set convergence.

assumptions_latex: \(C_n\) and \(C\) are nonempty compact subsets of \(\mathbb R^d\).
There is a compact set \(K\subset\mathbb R^d\) such that \(C_n\subset K\) for every \(n\in\mathbb N\) and \(C\subset K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{co}C_n\xrightarrow{PK}\operatorname{co}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convexification stability under a common compact bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(d\in\mathbb N\). If the nonempty compact sets \(C_n,C\subset\mathbb R^d\) lie in a common compact set and \(C_n\xrightarrow{PK}C\), then
\[
\operatorname{co}C_n\xrightarrow{PK}\operatorname{co}C.
\]
Moreover,
\[
d_H\!\left(\operatorname{co}C_n,\operatorname{co}C\right)\le d_H(C_n,C).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite-dimensional space, commonly compact-bounded nonempty compact sets retain their convergence after convexification, and convexification does not increase Hausdorff distance.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexification Stability

children.title: Hull–Limit Commutation
children.top_down_role: Commutation of hull operations with limiting processes.

assumptions_latex: For every \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(A_n\subset X\) and \(A\subset X\) are nonempty, and \(d_H(A_n,A)<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_H\!\left(\overline{\operatorname{co}}A_n,\overline{\operatorname{co}}A\right)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hausdorff-limit commutation for the closed-convex-hull operator in a normed space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For nonempty subsets \(A_n,A\) of a normed vector space with finite Hausdorff distance,
\[
d_H\!\left(\overline{\operatorname{co}}A_n,\overline{\operatorname{co}}A\right)\le d_H(A_n,A).
\]
Therefore, \(d_H(A_n,A)\to0\) entails \(d_H\!\left(\overline{\operatorname{co}}A_n,\overline{\operatorname{co}}A\right)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed-convex-hull operator is nonexpansive in Hausdorff distance and therefore commutes with Hausdorff limits having finite distance.
knowledge_statements.title: Hull–Limit Commutation

children.title: Nonclosed-Hull Boundary
children.top_down_role: Distinctions between convex hulls and closed convex hulls in limits.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is closed, but \(\operatorname{co}C\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A closed unbounded planar set whose ordinary convex hull omits a finite boundary point generated by convex combinations involving points escaping to infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(C\subset\mathbb R^2\) is closed, but its convex hull is not closed. Specifically, \((1,1/t^2)\in\operatorname{co}C\) for every \(t\ge1\), these points converge to \((1,0)\), and \((1,0)\notin\operatorname{co}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This closed unbounded planar set has a nonclosed convex hull with the missing boundary point (1,0).
knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed-Hull Boundary

assumptions_latex: For every \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(A_n=\{0\}\) and \(B_n=\{1/n\}\) are subsets of \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_n\xrightarrow{PK}\{0\}\) and \(B_n\xrightarrow{PK}\{0\}\), but \(A_n\cap B_n=\varnothing\) for every \(n\in\mathbb N\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary failure of intersection continuity caused by approaching sets with no persistent common point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sequences satisfy \(A_n\xrightarrow{PK}\{0\}\) and \(B_n\xrightarrow{PK}\{0\}\), whereas \(A_n\cap B_n=\varnothing\) for every \(n\in\mathbb N\). Thus
\[
A_n\cap B_n\xrightarrow{PK}\varnothing\ne\{0\}=\{0\}\cap\{0\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two set sequences can converge to the same singleton while every termwise intersection is empty, so intersection does not generally commute with set convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Intersection Instability

children.title: Image Escape
children.top_down_role: Image points escaping bounded observation regions.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset X\) is closed and \(f:X\to Y\) is continuous.
\((x_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}\) is a sequence in \(C\), and \(f(x_k)\to y\) for some \(y\in Y\setminus f(C)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sequence \((x_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}\) has no convergent subsequence in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential characterization of the escape mechanism producing a missing limit point in a continuous image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be closed and let \(f:X\to Y\) be continuous. If \(x_k\in C\) and \(f(x_k)\to y\) for some \(y\notin f(C)\), then \((x_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}\) has no convergent subsequence in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence of preimages approaching a missing limit point of a continuous image has no convergent subsequence in the closed domain set.
knowledge_statements.title: Image Escape

children.title: Closedness Loss
children.top_down_role: Failure of limiting images to retain closedness.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is closed, while \(f(C)=(0,\infty)\) is not closed in \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous maps need not preserve closedness when compactness or properness is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The set \(C=\mathbb R\) is closed and the map \(f(x)=e^x\) is continuous, but
\[
f(C)=(0,\infty)
\]
is not closed in \(\mathbb R\). In particular, \(f(-n)=e^{-n}\to0\) while \(0\notin f(C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential map sends the closed real line to the nonclosed positive half-line, so a continuous image of a closed set need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.title: Closedness Loss

children.title: Properness Recovery
children.top_down_role: Properness-based control of image escape and closedness.

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to Y\) is continuous and proper, meaning that \(f^{-1}(K)\) is compact for every compact set \(K\subset Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(C)\) is closed in \(Y\).

notation.meaning: inverse image of K under f

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-image recovery for continuous proper maps between metric spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be metric spaces. If \(f:X\to Y\) is continuous and proper, then \(f\) is a closed map: for every closed set \(C\subset X\), the image \(f(C)\) is closed in \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous proper map between metric spaces sends every closed set to a closed set.
knowledge_statements.title: Properness Recovery

children.title: Unbounded-Fiber Pathologies
children.top_down_role: Image instability caused by unbounded inverse fibers.

assumptions_latex: \(p:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) is the coordinate projection defined by \(p(x,y)=x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is closed, but \(p(C)=\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\) is not closed in \(\mathbb R\).

notation.meaning: inverse image of a set or point under p

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection example in which an unbounded sequence in a closed set has convergent images approaching a value missing from the image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The hyperbola \(C\) is closed and the projection \(p\) is continuous, but
\[
p(C)=\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}
\]
is not closed. The sequence \((1/k,k)\in C\) is unbounded, while \(p(1/k,k)=1/k\to0\notin p(C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unbounded sequence in the closed hyperbola escapes while its projections converge to zero, which is missing from the projected image.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Fiber Pathologies

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_n\xrightarrow{PK}C\), but \(d_H(C_n,C)=n\not\to0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Escaping components are invisible to Painlevé–Kuratowski limits but dominate global Hausdorff distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(C_n=\{0,n\}\) and \(C=\{0\}\),
\[
C_n\xrightarrow{PK}C,
\qquad
d_H(C_n,C)=n\to\infty.
\]
Thus Painlevé–Kuratowski convergence does not imply global Hausdorff convergence when components can escape to infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A component escaping to infinity disappears from the Painlevé–Kuratowski limit but makes the global Hausdorff distance diverge.
knowledge_statements.title: Global–Local Convergence Mismatch

children.title: Graph Limit Foundations
children.top_down_role: Foundational modes and structures for convergence of graphs.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_n\xrightarrow{g}F\iff \liminf_n\operatorname{gph}F_n=\operatorname{gph}F=\limsup_n\operatorname{gph}F_n.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential graph limits and graphical convergence for multifunctions between metric spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(n\), define \(G_n=\operatorname{gph}F_n=\{(x,y)\in X\times Y:y\in F_n(x)\}\). The graphical inner and outer limits are
\[
\operatorname*{g\!\!-liminf}_{n\to\infty}F_n:=\liminf_{n\to\infty}G_n,
\qquad
\operatorname*{g\!\!-limsup}_{n\to\infty}F_n:=\limsup_{n\to\infty}G_n.
\]
The sequence converges graphically to \(F\), written \(F_n\xrightarrow{g}F\), precisely when
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}G_n=\operatorname{gph}F=\limsup_{n\to\infty}G_n.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graphical convergence of multifunctions is Painlevé–Kuratowski convergence of their graphs in the product space.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph Limit Foundations

children.title: Set–Graph Limit Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Correspondences and distinctions between set limits and graph limits.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_n\to_g F\iff \operatorname{gph}F_n\to\operatorname{gph}F\) in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graphical convergence is represented as ordinary set convergence in the product space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(n\), regard \(F_n\) as the set \(\operatorname{gph}F_n:=\{(x,y)\in X\times Y:y\in F_n(x)\}\). Its graphical outer and inner limits are represented by \[\operatorname{gph}(\operatorname{g-limsup}F_n):=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{gph}F_n,\qquad \operatorname{gph}(\operatorname{g-liminf}F_n):=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{gph}F_n.\] Thus \(F_n\) converges graphically to \(F\) exactly when these two product-space set limits coincide with \(\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graphical limits of multifunctions are precisely Painlevé–Kuratowski limits of their graphs in the product space.
knowledge_statements.title: Set–Graph Limit Interfaces

children.title: Multifunction Convergence Calculus
children.top_down_role: Objects, continuity properties, convergence modes, compactness, metric representations, and convergence-preserving operations for multifunctions.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Continuity of set-valued maps; graphical and epigraphical convergence

children.title: Multifunction Graphs
children.top_down_role: Graph representations of set-valued mappings.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}F=\{(x,y)\in X\times Y:y\in F(x)\}\).

notation.meaning: set-valued mapping from X to Y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The graph encodes all incidences between arguments and values.

source_refs.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The graph of \(F\) is the subset of the product space defined by \[\operatorname{gph}F:=\{(x,y)\in X\times Y:y\in F(x)\}.\] Consequently, membership \(y\in F(x)\) is equivalent to the incidence relation \((x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction’s graph is the set of all argument–value pairs incident to the mapping.
knowledge_statements.title: Multifunction Graphs

source_witnesses.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

children.title: Graph Closures
children.top_down_role: Closure constructions applied to multifunction graphs.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}\overline F=\operatorname{cl}_{X\times Y}(\operatorname{gph}F)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure is taken jointly in arguments and values, not separately in each fiber.

source_refs.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The graph closure of \(F\) is the multifunction \(\overline F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) uniquely specified by \[\operatorname{gph}\overline F:=\operatorname{cl}_{X\times Y}(\operatorname{gph}F).\] Equivalently, \(\overline F(x):=\{y\in Y:(x,y)\in\operatorname{cl}_{X\times Y}(\operatorname{gph}F)\}\). In general, this joint closure can contain values generated by nearby arguments and need not equal \(\operatorname{cl}_Y F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graph closure is obtained by closing the entire graph in the product topology and then taking its vertical sections.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph Closures

source_witnesses.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

children.title: Closed-Graph Representations
children.top_down_role: Representation of multifunction behavior through closed graphs.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) has closed graph if and only if limits of convergent graph sequences remain in its graph.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential and closure representations agree in metric product spaces.

source_refs.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The following conditions are equivalent: \(\operatorname{gph}F\) is closed in \(X\times Y\); \(F=\overline F\); and, whenever \(x_k\to x\), \(y_k\to y\), and \(y_k\in F(x_k)\) for every \(k\), one has \(y\in F(x)\). Hence a closed-graph multifunction is exactly one represented by a closed incidence set in the product space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction has closed graph exactly when every convergent sequence of its argument–value pairs has its limit in the graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Graph Representations

source_witnesses.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^{-1}(y)=\{x\in X:y\in F(x)\}\) and \(\operatorname{gph}F^{-1}=\{(y,x):(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The inverse reverses the graph incidence relation and is generally set-valued.

source_refs.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The inverse multifunction \(F^{-1}:Y\rightrightarrows X\) is defined by \[F^{-1}(y):=\{x\in X:y\in F(x)\}.\] Thus \(x\in F^{-1}(y)\) if and only if \(y\in F(x)\), and its graph is the coordinate transpose \[\operatorname{gph}F^{-1}=\tau(\operatorname{gph}F)=\{(y,x)\in Y\times X:(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inverse multifunction assigns to each value all arguments whose images contain that value; its graph is the transposed original graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse Multifunctions

source_witnesses.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

children.title: Multifunction Domains
children.top_down_role: Domain structure of set-valued mappings.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}F=\{x\in X:F(x)\ne\varnothing\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The effective domain records arguments having at least one incident graph value.

source_refs.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The effective domain of \(F\) is \[\operatorname{dom}F:=\{x\in X:F(x)\ne\varnothing\}=\{x\in X:\exists y\in Y,\ (x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\}.\] Arguments outside \(\operatorname{dom}F\) have empty multifunction value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The domain consists exactly of arguments at which the multifunction has a nonempty value.
knowledge_statements.title: Multifunction Domains

source_witnesses.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

children.title: Multifunction Ranges
children.top_down_role: Range structure of set-valued mappings.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rge}F=\bigcup_{x\in X}F(x)=\operatorname{dom}F^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The range collects all values attained at any argument.

source_refs.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The range of \(F\) is \[\operatorname{rge}F:=\{y\in Y:\exists x\in X,\ y\in F(x)\}=\bigcup_{x\in X}F(x).\] Equivalently, \(\operatorname{rge}F=\operatorname{dom}F^{-1}\), because a value is attained by \(F\) exactly when its inverse fiber is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The range is the union of all multifunction values and equals the domain of the inverse multifunction.
knowledge_statements.title: Multifunction Ranges

source_witnesses.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

children.title: Multifunction Images
children.top_down_role: Images of points or sets under multifunctions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(A)=\bigcup_{x\in A}F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the direct image of a subset under a set-valued mapping.

source_refs.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The image of \(A\) under \(F\) is \[F(A):=\{y\in Y:\exists x\in A,\ y\in F(x)\}=\bigcup_{x\in A}F(x).\] In graph form, \(F(A)\) is the projection onto \(Y\) of \(\operatorname{gph}F\cap(A\times Y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The image of a set is the union of the multifunction values over all arguments in that set.
knowledge_statements.title: Multifunction Images

source_witnesses.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

children.title: Multifunction Fibers
children.top_down_role: Fiber structure associated with target values.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^{-1}(y)=\{x\in X:(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A fiber is the horizontal section of the graph at a fixed value.

source_refs.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The fiber of \(F\) over \(y\) is the inverse value \[F^{-1}(y):=\{x\in X:y\in F(x)\}=\{x\in X:(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\}.\] It is nonempty exactly when \(y\in\operatorname{rge}F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fiber over a value contains precisely the arguments whose multifunction values contain that value.
knowledge_statements.title: Multifunction Fibers

source_witnesses.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

children.title: Outer Semicontinuity
children.top_down_role: Outer-semicontinuous behavior of multifunctions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is outer semicontinuous at \(\bar x\) if \(\limsup_{x\to\bar x}F(x)\subset F(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: outer limit of values as x approaches the reference point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential outer semicontinuity in metric spaces is used.

source_refs.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The multifunction \(F\) is outer semicontinuous at \(\bar x\) when \[\limsup_{x\to\bar x}F(x):=\{y\in Y:\exists x_k\to\bar x,\ \exists y_k\to y,\ y_k\in F(x_k)\}\subset F(\bar x).\] Equivalently, every convergent sequence of graph points \((x_k,y_k)\in\operatorname{gph}F\) with \(x_k\to\bar x\) has its limit \((\bar x,y)\) in \(\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer semicontinuity means every limit of values taken at nearby arguments remains a value at the reference argument.
knowledge_statements.title: Outer Semicontinuity

source_witnesses.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sequential formulation is mathematically coherent, but the cited locator is the section on domains, ranges, and inverses rather than a continuity section. Because outer-semicontinuity terminology varies across sources, a locator explicitly supporting this convention and equivalence is required.

children.title: Closed-Graph Regimes
children.top_down_role: Closedness properties of multifunction graphs.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is outer semicontinuous on \(X\) if and only if \(\operatorname{gph}F\) is closed in \(X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global sequential outer semicontinuity is equivalent to a globally closed graph.

source_refs.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose outer semicontinuity is understood sequentially. Then \(F\) is outer semicontinuous at every \(x\in X\), meaning \(\limsup_{u\to x}F(u)\subset F(x)\), if and only if \(\operatorname{gph}F\) is closed in \(X\times Y\). Equivalently, every convergent sequence \((x_k,y_k)\in\operatorname{gph}F\) has its product-space limit in \(\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For multifunctions between metric spaces, outer semicontinuity at every point is equivalent to closedness of the entire graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Graph Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: A. Domains, Ranges and Inverses p. 149

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is correct under the stated sequential metric-space convention and its content kind fits Closed-Graph Regimes. The supplied domains-and-inverses locator does not inspectably support the outer-semicontinuity equivalence, so a relevant theorem or continuity-section citation is required.

children.title: Local Boundedness Interface
children.top_down_role: Role of local boundedness in linking graph closure to outer semicontinuity.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space and \(Y\) is finite-dimensional normed.
\(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is locally bounded at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Outer semicontinuity at \(\bar x\) is equivalent to upper semicontinuity at \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: open neighborhood of the reference argument
open set containing the reference value set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional local boundedness supplies compactness needed for the neighborhood characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated assumptions, \(F\) is outer semicontinuous at \(\bar x\) if and only if it is upper semicontinuous there in the neighborhood sense: for every open set \(V\subset Y\) satisfying \(F(\bar x)\subset V\), there exists a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that \(F(x)\subset V\) for every \(x\in U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For locally bounded finite-dimensional-valued multifunctions with a closed nonempty reference value, outer and neighborhood upper semicontinuity coincide.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Boundedness Interface

children.title: Closed-Graph Equivalence Boundary
children.top_down_role: Settings where closed graphs do not fully characterize outer semicontinuity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{gph}F\text{ is closed}\iff F\text{ is outer semicontinuous at every }x\in X
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes the pointwise graph-limit condition from the corresponding global closed-graph assertion.

source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(\bar x\in X\), outer semicontinuity of \(F\) at \(\bar x\) means \(\operatorname*{Limsup}_{x\to\bar x}F(x)\subset F(\bar x)\), equivalently: whenever \(x_n\to\bar x\), \(y_n\to y\), and \(y_n\in F(x_n)\), one has \(y\in F(\bar x)\). Consequently, \(\operatorname{gph}F\) is closed in \(X\times Y\) if and only if this condition holds at every \(\bar x\in X\). At one fixed point it describes only graph limits whose first coordinates approach that point; it is not a global closed-graph assertion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer semicontinuity is the closed-graph limit condition at one base point. Requiring it at every point is equivalent to the graph being closed.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Graph Equivalence Boundary

source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

children.title: Inner Semicontinuity
children.top_down_role: Inner-semicontinuous behavior of multifunctions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is inner semicontinuous at }\bar x\iff F(\bar x)\subset\operatorname*{Liminf}_{x\to\bar x}F(x)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential metric-space definition; empty values make the condition vacuous at the reference point.

source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The multifunction \(F\) is inner semicontinuous at \(\bar x\) when, for every sequence \(x_n\to\bar x\) and every \(y\in F(\bar x)\), there exist points \(y_n\in F(x_n)\) such that \(y_n\to y\). Equivalently, \[F(\bar x)\subset\operatorname*{Liminf}_{x\to\bar x}F(x).\] Inner semicontinuity on a set \(D\subset X\) means inner semicontinuity at every \(\bar x\in D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every value at the reference point must be approximable by values chosen from every sequence of nearby images.
knowledge_statements.title: Inner Semicontinuity

source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

children.title: Lower-Continuity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Lower-continuity formulations across topological settings.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is lower continuous at }\bar x\iff \forall V\subset Y\text{ open},\ F(\bar x)\cap V\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow \bar x\in\operatorname{int}F^{-1}(V)

notation.meaning: Lower inverse image of a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses lower continuity in the standard lower-hemicontinuity sense for multifunctions.

source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The multifunction \(F\) is lower continuous at \( ar x\) if, for every open set \(V\subset Y\) satisfying \(F( ar x)\cap V
e\varnothing\), there exists a neighborhood \(U\) of \( ar x\) such that \(F(x)\cap V
e\varnothing\) for every \(x\in U\). Equivalently, with \(F^{-1}(V):=\{x\in X:F(x)\cap V
e\varnothing\}\), one has \( ar x\in\operatorname{int}F^{-1}(V)\) for every such \(V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every open set meeting the reference image must continue to meet all images at sufficiently nearby points.
knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Continuity Regimes

source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

children.title: Open-Set Characterizations
children.top_down_role: Topological characterizations based on inverse images of open-set incidence.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is lower continuous on }X\iff F^{-1}(V)\text{ is open for every open }V\subset Y

notation.meaning: Lower inverse image of a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global open-set characterization of lower continuity.

source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an open set \(V\subset Y\), define its lower inverse image by \(F^{-1}(V):=\{x\in X:F(x)\cap V\ne\varnothing\}\). Then \(F\) is lower continuous at every point of \(X\) if and only if \(F^{-1}(V)\) is open in \(X\) for every open \(V\subset Y\). Pointwise at \(\bar x\in X\), the equivalent condition is that every such lower inverse image containing \(\bar x\) is a neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower continuity holds globally exactly when the lower inverse image of every open subset of the range is open.
knowledge_statements.title: Open-Set Characterizations

source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

children.title: Lower-Continuity Equivalence Boundary
children.top_down_role: Settings where common lower-continuity formulations diverge.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is lower continuous at }\bar x\iff\text{ sequential inner semicontinuity holds at }\bar x
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First countability of the domain supports detection of failed lower continuity by sequences, while first countability of the range supports constructing selections converging to a prescribed image point.

source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If both \(X\) and \(Y\) are first countable, lower continuity of \(F\) at \(\bar x\) is equivalent to the following sequential condition: for every sequence \(x_n\to\bar x\) and every \(y\in F(\bar x)\), there exist \(y_n\in F(x_n)\) such that \(y_n\to y\). Without suitable sequentiality assumptions on the domain and a countable local base at the prescribed range point, this sequence-and-selection formulation need not characterize the general topological notion of lower continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sequence-and-selection characterization follows under first countability of both the domain and range; general topological spaces require an open-set or suitably formulated net characterization.
knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Continuity Equivalence Boundary

source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is locally bounded at }\bar x\iff\exists U\ni\bar x,\ \sup\{\|y\|:x\in U,\ y\in F(x)\}<\infty

notation.meaning: Union of images over a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normed-range definition at a reference point.

source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The multifunction \(F\) is locally bounded at \(\bar x\in X\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a bounded set \(B\subset Y\) such that \(F(x)\subset B\) for every \(x\in U\). Equivalently, \[\sup\{\|y\|:x\in U,\ y\in F(x)\}<\infty\] for some neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\), with the supremum of the empty set interpreted as \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction is locally bounded when all values over some neighborhood lie in one bounded subset of the range.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Boundedness of Multifunctions

source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

children.title: Total Continuity
children.top_down_role: Total-continuity regimes for multifunctions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is totally continuous at }\bar x\iff \forall x_n\to\bar x,\ F(x_n)\xrightarrow{K}F(\bar x)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential total continuity expressed as Kuratowski convergence of every nearby image sequence.

source_refs.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The multifunction \(F\) is totally continuous at \(\bar x\) if, for every sequence \(x_n\to\bar x\), its images converge to \(F(\bar x)\) in the Kuratowski sense: \[\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}F(x_n)=F(\bar x)=\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}F(x_n).\] In metric spaces this is equivalent to simultaneous outer and inner semicontinuity at \(\bar x\). Total continuity on \(D\subset X\) means this condition holds at every point of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every sequence of nearby images must converge in the Kuratowski sense to the image at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.title: Total Continuity

source_witnesses.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Kuratowski image-limit formula is coherent, but the cited locators do not presently establish that this condition is called `total continuity`, nor that the claimed equivalence with simultaneous outer and inner semicontinuity is intended at this level of generality. Source inspection is required before choosing a mathematically and terminologically reliable version.

children.title: Compact-Valued Regimes
children.top_down_role: Continuity behavior specialized to compact-valued mappings.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(\bar x)\text{ is compact and }F\text{ is outer semicontinuous at }\bar x

notation.meaning: Open and closed balls centered at the reference point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional compactness regime coupling bounded nearby values with an explicit local closed-graph condition.

source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose there exists \(r>0\) such that \(\bigcup_{x\in B(\bar x,r)}F(x)\) is bounded and \(\operatorname{gph}F\cap(\overline B(\bar x,r)\times Y)\) is closed. Then \(F(\bar x)\) is compact and \(F\) is outer semicontinuous at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a finite-dimensional range, bounded nearby values together with the stated local closed-graph condition yield a compact reference value and outer semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Valued Regimes

source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

children.title: Sequential Compactness Interface
children.top_down_role: Interaction between total continuity and compactness of value selections.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is locally bounded at }\bar x\iff\forall x_n\to\bar x,\ \forall y_n\in F(x_n),\ (y_n)\text{ has a convergent subsequence}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional sequential characterization, quantified over every full selection from images along a convergent base sequence.

source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The multifunction \(F\) is locally bounded at \(\bar x\) if and only if, for every sequence \(x_n\to\bar x\) and every sequence satisfying \(y_n\in F(x_n)\) for all \(n\), the sequence \((y_n)\) has a convergent subsequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a finite-dimensional range, local boundedness is equivalent to sequential precompactness of every full selection from images along a convergent base sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Compactness Interface

source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

children.title: Multifunction Convergence Modes
children.top_down_role: The principal convergence modes for multifunctions and the distinctions among imagewise and graphwise limits.

children.title: Pointwise Convergence of Multifunctions
children.top_down_role: Imagewise set convergence at fixed arguments.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{iwK}}F\iff\forall x\in X,\ \operatorname*{Liminf}_nF_n(x)=F(x)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_nF_n(x)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise convergence of fixed-base images in the Kuratowski sense.

source_refs.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence \((F_n)\) converges imagewise in the Kuratowski sense to \(F\) when, for every fixed \(x\in X\), \[\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}F_n(x)=F(x)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}F_n(x).\] Equivalently, every \(y\in F(x)\) is the limit of some sequence \(y_n\in F_n(x)\), while every convergent subsequence \(y_{n_k}\in F_{n_k}(x)\) has its limit in \(F(x)\). The base point remains fixed throughout both tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each fixed base point, the images converge to the limiting image through matching inner and outer Kuratowski limits.
knowledge_statements.title: Imagewise Kuratowski Convergence

source_witnesses.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

assumptions_latex: F_n,F:X\rightrightarrows Y\text{ have nonempty compact values}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{pH}}F\iff\forall x\in X,\ d_H(F_n(x),F(x))\to0
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defined for nonempty compact-valued multifunctions using the Hausdorff metric on each image.

source_refs.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence \((F_n)\) converges pointwise in Hausdorff distance to \(F\) if, for every fixed \(x\in X\), \[d_H(F_n(x),F(x))\longrightarrow0,\] where \[d_H(A,B):=\max\left\{\sup_{a\in A}d(a,B),\ \sup_{b\in B}d(b,A)\right\}.\] Thus the convergence is tested separately on each image and imposes no uniformity in \(x\). For compact subsets of \(Y\), Hausdorff convergence implies Kuratowski convergence of the corresponding fixed-base images.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every fixed base point, the compact images approach the limiting image in Hausdorff distance, without uniformity across base points.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Hausdorff Convergence

source_witnesses.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in\mathbb R,\ F_n(x)\xrightarrow{H}F(x)\quad\text{but}\quad\operatorname{gph}F_n\not\xrightarrow{K}\operatorname{gph}F
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A moving-spike counterexample separating pointwise image convergence from graphical convergence.

source_refs.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(F(x):=\{0\}\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R\), and define \[F_n(x):=\begin{cases}\{1\},&x=1/n,\\\{0\},&x\ne 1/n.\end{cases}\] Then, for every fixed \(x\in\mathbb R\), \(F_n(x)\) converges to \(F(x)\) in Hausdorff distance, whereas \[\operatorname{gph}F_n\xrightarrow{K}\operatorname{gph}F\cup\{(0,1)\}\ne\operatorname{gph}F.\] Thus pointwise image convergence does not imply graphical convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spike moving toward the origin disappears at every fixed base point but produces an additional graphical limit point at (0,1).
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise–Graphical Convergence Gap

source_witnesses.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

children.title: Graphical Convergence
children.top_down_role: Convergence induced by set convergence of complete multifunction graphs.

children.title: Graphical Inner Limits
children.top_down_role: Inner limits of multifunction graphs.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are metric spaces, and \(F_n:X\rightrightarrows Y\).
The product \(Z=X\times Y\) carries a compatible product metric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{gph}\!\left(\operatorname{g\!\!-liminf}_{n\to\infty}F_n\right)=\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{gph}F_n.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential graphical inner limit for multifunctions between metric spaces.

source_refs.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166
A. Inner and Outer Limits p. 109

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For multifunctions \(F_n:X\rightrightarrows Y\), the graphical inner limit is the multifunction whose graph is the Painlevé-Kuratowski inner limit of the graphs. Explicitly, \((x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}(\operatorname{g\!\!-liminf}_{n\to\infty}F_n)\) exactly when there are points \((x_n,y_n)\in\operatorname{gph}F_n\), for every sufficiently large \(n\), such that \((x_n,y_n)\to(x,y)\). Equivalently, \(d((x,y),\operatorname{gph}F_n)\to0\), with distance to the empty set interpreted as \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graphical inner limit contains precisely the graph points approximable by graph points of every sufficiently late multifunction.
knowledge_statements.title: Graphical Inner Limits

source_witnesses.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166
A. Inner and Outer Limits p. 109

children.title: Graphical Outer Limits
children.top_down_role: Outer limits of multifunction graphs.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are metric spaces, and \(F_n:X\rightrightarrows Y\).
The product \(Z=X\times Y\) carries a compatible product metric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{gph}\!\left(\operatorname{g\!\!-limsup}_{n\to\infty}F_n\right)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{gph}F_n.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential graphical outer limit for multifunctions between metric spaces.

source_refs.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166
A. Inner and Outer Limits p. 109

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For multifunctions \(F_n:X\rightrightarrows Y\), the graphical outer limit is the multifunction whose graph is the Painlevé-Kuratowski outer limit of the graphs. Explicitly, \((x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}(\operatorname{g\!\!-limsup}_{n\to\infty}F_n)\) exactly when some strictly increasing sequence \((n_k)\) and points \((x_k,y_k)\in\operatorname{gph}F_{n_k}\) satisfy \((x_k,y_k)\to(x,y)\). Thus it records every cluster point obtainable along a subsequence of graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graphical outer limit contains precisely the limits of graph points selected along subsequences of the multifunction sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Graphical Outer Limits

source_witnesses.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166
A. Inner and Outer Limits p. 109

children.title: Two-Sided Graphical Convergence
children.top_down_role: Agreement of graphical inner and outer limiting behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are metric spaces, and \(F_n,F:X\rightrightarrows Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{gph}F_n=\operatorname{gph}F=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{gph}F_n.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Painlevé–Kuratowski convergence of graphs in the product space.

source_refs.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence \((F_n)\) converges graphically to \(F\), written \(F_n\xrightarrow{g}F\), when its graphical inner and outer limits coincide with \(F\). Equivalently, every \((x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\) is approximated by points \((x_n,y_n)\in\operatorname{gph}F_n\), while every convergent subsequence \((x_k,y_k)\in\operatorname{gph}F_{n_k}\) has its limit in \(\operatorname{gph}F\). The graphical limit, when it exists, is uniquely determined by its graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two-sided graphical convergence means that the inner and outer set limits of the graphs both equal the graph of the limit multifunction.
knowledge_statements.title: Two-Sided Graphical Convergence

source_witnesses.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

children.title: Inverse Multifunction Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Symmetry between a multifunction and its inverse.

notation.meaning: Inverse multifunction from Y to X

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued inversion without injectivity or surjectivity assumptions.

source_refs.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(y\in Y\), define the inverse value by \(F^{-1}(y)=\{x\in X:y\in F(x)\}\). Then inversion is involutive: for every \(x\in X\), \((F^{-1})^{-1}(x)=F(x)\). Moreover, \(y\in F(x)\) if and only if \(x\in F^{-1}(y)\). These identities hold for arbitrary set-valued mappings, including mappings with empty values, and require neither single-valuedness nor any regularity assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set-valued inversion exchanges inputs and outputs and is involutive, even when values are empty or contain multiple points.
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse Multifunction Symmetry

source_witnesses.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

children.title: Graph Transposition
children.top_down_role: Coordinate transposition of multifunction graphs.

assumptions_latex: \(T:X\times Y\to Y\times X\) is defined by \(T(x,y)=(y,x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{gph}F^{-1}=T(\operatorname{gph}F)=\{(y,x):(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph identity induced by exchanging product coordinates.

source_refs.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every multifunction \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), the graph of its inverse is the coordinate transpose of its graph: \(\operatorname{gph}F^{-1}=T(\operatorname{gph}F)=\{(y,x):(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\}\). The transposition map \(T\) is bijective and involutive, with \(T^{-1}=T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inverse multifunction's graph is exactly the original graph with its input and output coordinates exchanged.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph Transposition

source_witnesses.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

children.title: Convergence Invariance
children.top_down_role: Preservation of graphical convergence under inversion or transposition.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are metric spaces, and \(F_n,F:X\rightrightarrows Y\).
Both product spaces carry compatible product metrics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F_n\xrightarrow{g}F\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F_n^{-1}\xrightarrow{g}F^{-1}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariance of two-sided graphical convergence under multifunction inversion.

source_refs.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:X\times Y\to Y\times X\) be given by \(T(x,y)=(y,x)\). Then \(\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{gph}F_n^{-1}=T(\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{gph}F_n)\) and \(\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{gph}F_n^{-1}=T(\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{gph}F_n)\). In particular, \(F_n\xrightarrow{g}F\) if and only if \(F_n^{-1}\xrightarrow{g}F^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graphical inner limits, outer limits, and two-sided graphical convergence are invariant under inversion because the associated graphs are coordinate transposes.
knowledge_statements.title: Convergence Invariance

source_witnesses.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

children.title: Inverse-Symmetry Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Settings where related non-graphical convergence modes lose inverse symmetry.

assumptions_latex: For \(n\ge1\), define \(F_n:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\) by \(F_n(1/n)=\{0\}\) and \(F_n(x)=\varnothing\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F_n(x)\to F(x)\text{ for every fixed }x,\qquad F_n^{-1}(0)=\{1/n\}\to\{0\}\ne F^{-1}(0).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise convergence lacks the inversion symmetry enjoyed by graphical convergence.

source_refs.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each fixed \(x\in\mathbb R\), one has \(F_n(x)=\varnothing\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), so the values converge pointwise to \(F(x)=\varnothing\). At \(y=0\), however, \(F_n^{-1}(0)=\{1/n\}\), whose set limit is \(\{0\}\), whereas \(F^{-1}(0)=\varnothing\). Hence inversion need not preserve pointwise set convergence. The missing hypothesis is convergence of the entire graphs, which detects the moving points \((1/n,0)\to(0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise set convergence is not invariant under inversion: moving graph points can disappear at every fixed input but persist after inversion.
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Symmetry Failure Boundary

source_witnesses.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

children.title: Localized Graph Convergence
children.top_down_role: Graph convergence observed on bounded or local regions.

assumptions_latex: \((Z,\rho)\) is a metric space with base point \(z_0\), and \(G_n,G\subset Z\) are closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[G_n\to_{m loc}G\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sup_{z\in B_r}\left|\min\{1,d(z,G_n)\}-\min\{1,d(z,G)\}\right|\to0\quad\forall r>0.\]

notation.meaning: Closed metric ball of radius r about z_0

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local uniform convergence of truncated distance functions for closed graphs.

source_refs.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For closed sets \(G_n,G\subset Z\), localized convergence means uniform convergence on every bounded observation ball of their truncated distance functions. With the convention \(d(z,\varnothing)=+\infty\), this definition also permits empty sets. For multifunctions \(F_n,F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) having closed graphs, localized graph convergence is defined by applying this criterion in \(Z=X\times Y\) to \(G_n=\operatorname{gph}F_n\) and \(G=\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed graphs converge locally when their truncated distance functions converge uniformly on every bounded observation ball.
knowledge_statements.title: Localized Graph Convergence

source_witnesses.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

children.title: Metric Graph Convergence
children.top_down_role: Metric realizations of convergence between multifunction graphs.

assumptions_latex: \((Z,\rho)\) is a metric space with base point \(z_0\), and \(G,H\subset Z\) are closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[D(G,H)=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}2^{-m}\delta_m(G,H),\qquad G_n\to_{\rm loc}G\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad D(G_n,G)\to0.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A summable metric representation of local closed-graph convergence.

source_refs.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(D(G,H)=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}2^{-m}\delta_m(G,H)\). On the family of closed subsets of \(Z\), including the empty set, \(D\) is a metric. For closed sets \(G_n,G\subset Z\), \(D(G_n,G)\to0\) if and only if \(\delta_m(G_n,G)\to0\) for every integer \(m\ge1\), equivalently \(G_n\to_{\rm loc}G\). Applied to closed graphs, \(D\) metrizes localized graph convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted sum of bounded-window distance-function discrepancies is a metric that metrizes localized convergence of closed graphs.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Graph Convergence

source_witnesses.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

children.title: Bounded-Window Graph Metrics
children.top_down_role: Graph metrics formed through bounded observation windows.

assumptions_latex: \((Z,\rho)\) is a metric space with base point \(z_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\delta_r(G,H)=\sup_{\rho(z,z_0)\le r}\left|\min\{1,d(z,G)\}-\min\{1,d(z,H)\}\right|\in[0,1].\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Truncated distance-function discrepancy on a bounded observation window.

source_refs.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For radius \(r>0\), the bounded-window discrepancy between closed sets \(G\) and \(H\) is the uniform difference of their truncated distance functions over \(B_r(z_0)\). Use \(d(z,\varnothing)=+\infty\), so \(\min\{1,d(z,\varnothing)\}=1\). The quantity \(\delta_r\) is symmetric, nonnegative, bounded by \(1\), and satisfies the triangle inequality, although a single fixed window may fail to distinguish sets whose distance functions agree throughout that window.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-window graph discrepancy compares truncated distances to two closed graphs only from points within a fixed observation ball.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Window Graph Metrics

source_witnesses.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

children.title: Graph-Convergence Globalization Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits of passing from localized graph convergence to global convergence.

assumptions_latex: Localized convergence is measured by bounded-window truncated distance discrepancies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[G_n\to_{\rm loc}G,\qquad d_H(G_n,G)=n\not\to0.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local graph convergence does not control graph components escaping to infinity.

source_refs.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(r>0\). Whenever \(n>2r\), every \(z\in[-r,r]\) is at least as close to \(0\) as to \(n\), hence \(d(z,G_n)=d(z,G)\) and \(\delta_r(G_n,G)=0\). Thus \(G_n\to_{\rm loc}G\). Nevertheless, the global Hausdorff excess of \(G_n\) over \(G\) equals \(d(n,G)=n\), so \(d_H(G_n,G)=n\). Local convergence globalizes only with additional control preventing graph points from escaping beyond all bounded windows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local convergence ignores components escaping to infinity, so it need not imply global Hausdorff convergence without a uniform boundedness condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Convergence Globalization Boundary

source_witnesses.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are metric spaces, and \(f_n,f:X\to Y\) are single-valued maps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f_n\xrightarrow{c}f\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \bigl(\forall x\in X\;\forall (x_n)\subset X:\ x_n\to x\implies f_n(x_n)\to f(x)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential continuous convergence of metric-space-valued functions.

source_refs.locator: G. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 175
C. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 250

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence \((f_n)\) converges continuously to \(f\), written \(f_n\xrightarrow{c}f\), when for every \(x\in X\) and every sequence \((x_n)\subset X\) satisfying \(x_n\to x\), one has \(f_n(x_n)\to f(x)\). Continuous convergence implies pointwise convergence, and its limit map \(f\) is continuous. Continuity of the individual maps \(f_n\) is not required by the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous convergence requires output convergence along every convergent sequence of moving inputs; it implies pointwise convergence and continuity of the limit without requiring the approximating maps to be continuous.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Convergence

source_witnesses.locator: G. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 175
C. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 250

children.title: Compact-Uniform Convergence
children.top_down_role: Uniform convergence restricted to compact subsets of the domain.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological space and \((Y,d_Y)\) is a metric space.
\(F_n,F:X\to\mathcal K(Y)\), where \(\mathcal K(Y)\) denotes the nonempty compact subsets of \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_n\to F\) compact-uniformly exactly when the displayed convergence holds for every compact \(K\subset X\).

notation.meaning: Hausdorff distance induced by the metric on Y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hausdorff-valued compact-uniform convergence on the domain.

source_refs.locator: G. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 175

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sequence \((F_n)\) converges compact-uniformly to \(F\) if, for every compact set \(K\subset X\),
\[
\sup_{x\in K}d_H\bigl(F_n(x),F(x)\bigr)\longrightarrow 0.
\]
The empty compact set imposes no condition, with its supremum conventionally equal to \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compact-uniform convergence means that the Hausdorff error between the multifunction values tends uniformly to zero on every compact subset of the domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Uniform Convergence

source_witnesses.locator: G. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 175

children.title: Locally Uniform Convergence
children.top_down_role: Uniform convergence organized through neighborhoods or local domain regions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological space and \((Y,d_Y)\) is a metric space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_n\to F\) locally uniformly exactly when every point admits a neighborhood satisfying the displayed uniform estimate.

notation.meaning: Hausdorff distance induced by the metric on Y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local uniformity is measured by Hausdorff distance between values.

source_refs.locator: G. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 175

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sequence \((F_n)\) converges locally uniformly to \(F\) if, for every \(x\in X\), there exists a neighborhood \(U_x\) of \(x\), independent of \(n\), such that
\[
\sup_{u\in U_x}d_H\bigl(F_n(u),F(u)\bigr)\longrightarrow 0.
\]
The neighborhood may depend on \(x\), while the convergence is uniform over all points of that neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local uniform convergence requires uniform Hausdorff convergence on some fixed neighborhood of each domain point.
knowledge_statements.title: Locally Uniform Convergence

source_witnesses.locator: G. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 175

children.title: Compact-Exhaustion Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Relations between compact-uniform convergence, local uniformity, and exhaustion-based formulations.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological space and \((Y,d_Y)\) is a metric space.
\((K_m)_{m\ge1}\) is an increasing compact exhaustion cofinal among compact subsets of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local uniform convergence implies compact-uniform convergence; exhaustion convergence characterizes compact-uniform convergence, and local compactness makes the local and compact-uniform modes equivalent.

notation.meaning: Hausdorff distance on nonempty compact subsets of Y
An increasing compact exhaustion of X

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison under a compact exhaustion; local compactness supplies the converse implication.

source_refs.locator: G. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 175

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(F_n\to F\) locally uniformly, then \(F_n\to F\) compact-uniformly. Moreover,
\[
F_n\to F\text{ compact-uniformly}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\sup_{x\in K_m}d_H\bigl(F_n(x),F(x)\bigr)\to0
\text{ for every }m.
\]
If, in addition, every point of \(X\) has a compact neighborhood, then compact-uniform convergence also implies locally uniform convergence; hence the two modes coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local uniform convergence implies compact-uniform convergence. A cofinal compact exhaustion tests compact-uniform convergence, and local compactness makes the two notions equivalent.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Exhaustion Comparisons

source_witnesses.locator: G. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 175

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a nonempty set and \((Y,d_Y)\) is a metric space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_n\to F\) globally uniformly exactly when the supremal Hausdorff error over all of \(X\) tends to zero.

notation.meaning: Hausdorff distance induced by the metric on Y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global Hausdorff-uniform convergence of compact-valued multifunctions.

source_refs.locator: G. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 175

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sequence \((F_n)\) converges globally uniformly to \(F\) when
\[
\sup_{x\in X}d_H\bigl(F_n(x),F(x)\bigr)\longrightarrow0.
\]
Equivalently, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(N\) such that \(d_H(F_n(x),F(x))<\varepsilon\) for every \(x\in X\) and every \(n\ge N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global uniform convergence means that the largest Hausdorff error over the entire domain tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Global Uniform Convergence

source_witnesses.locator: G. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 175

children.title: Metric Descriptions of Multifunction Convergence
children.top_down_role: Metric representations of imagewise and graphical convergence.

children.title: Graph-Distance Constructions
children.top_down_role: Distance descriptions applied to complete multifunction graphs.

assumptions_latex: \((Z,d)\) is a proper metric space with base point \(z_0\).
\(F,G:X\rightrightarrows Y\) have nonempty closed graphs, viewed as closed subsets of \(Z=X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed quantity is a metric on nonempty closed graphs and measures locally uniform convergence of their distance functions.

notation.meaning: Distance from z to the graph of F
Closed ball in Z centered at the base point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attouch–Wets-type metric constructed from graph-distance functions.

source_refs.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each nonempty closed graph define \(\delta_F(z)=d(z,\operatorname{gph}F)\). The graph-distance metric
\[
D_{\mathrm{gd}}(F,G)=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}2^{-m}\min\!\left\{1,\sup_{z\in B_m}|\delta_F(z)-\delta_G(z)|\right\}
\]
is finite and vanishes exactly when \(\operatorname{gph}F=\operatorname{gph}G\). Thus graph convergence can be represented as \(D_{\mathrm{gd}}(F_n,F)\to0\), equivalently as uniform convergence of the graph-distance functions on every bounded ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted sum of local sup-norm differences between graph-distance functions defines a metric for closed multifunction graphs.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Distance Constructions

source_witnesses.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

children.title: Truncated-Graph Metrics
children.top_down_role: Localized graph metrics based on bounded truncation regions.

assumptions_latex: \((Z,d)\) is a metric space with base point \(z_0\).
\(F,G:X\rightrightarrows Y\) have nonempty closed graphs in \(Z=X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat d_r\) is a finite symmetric graph discrepancy at radius \(r\), and its zero value records mutual inclusion inside the truncation ball.

notation.meaning: Closed radius-r ball centered at the base point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary-stable truncation using excess to the full opposing graph.

source_refs.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
With \(e(\varnothing,B)=0\), the radius-\(r\) truncated-graph discrepancy is
\[
\widehat d_r(F,G)=\max\!\left\{e\bigl(\operatorname{gph}F\cap B_r,\operatorname{gph}G\bigr),e\bigl(\operatorname{gph}G\cap B_r,\operatorname{gph}F\bigr)\right\}.
\]
Unlike the Hausdorff distance between two separately truncated graphs, each truncated portion is compared with the full opposing graph, avoiding artificial discrepancies caused solely by cutting near the boundary of \(B_r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The truncated-graph discrepancy symmetrizes excesses from each graph inside a bounded ball to the full opposing graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Truncated-Graph Metrics

source_witnesses.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

children.title: Truncation-Radius Dependence
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of metric descriptions to the chosen truncation scale.

assumptions_latex: \((Z,d)\) is a metric space with base point \(z_0\).
\(F_n,F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) have nonempty closed graphs in \(Z=X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convergence of every fixed-radius discrepancy is equivalent to convergence along any unbounded increasing sequence of radii.

notation.meaning: Symmetric truncated-graph discrepancy at radius r
An unbounded increasing sequence of truncation radii

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Radius monotonicity makes any unbounded radius exhaustion convergence-determining.

source_refs.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The truncated discrepancy is monotone in its radius:
\[
0<r\le s\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \widehat d_r(F,G)\le\widehat d_s(F,G).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\widehat d_r(F_n,F)\to0\text{ for every }r>0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\widehat d_{r_j}(F_n,F)\to0\text{ for every }j.
\]
Thus the resulting convergence mode does not depend on the particular unbounded increasing radius sequence used to test it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Truncated-graph discrepancies increase with radius, so convergence can be tested on any fixed unbounded sequence of radii.
knowledge_statements.title: Truncation-Radius Dependence

source_witnesses.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

children.title: Image-Excess Profiles
children.top_down_role: Directional excess measurements for images of multifunctions.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d_X)\) and \((Y,d_Y)\) are metric spaces, with base point \(x_0\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The profile \(E_r(F\mid G)\) records the worst directed image excess over inputs in the radius-\(r\) ball.

notation.meaning: Excess of A over B in Y
Closed radius-r ball in X centered at x_0

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed, radius-indexed discrepancy between multifunction images.

source_refs.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(r>0\), the directed image-excess profile of \(F\) relative to \(G\) is
\[
E_r(F\mid G)=\sup_{x\in B_X(r)}e_Y\bigl(F(x),G(x)\bigr),
\qquad
e_Y(A,B)=\sup_{a\in A}\inf_{b\in B}d_Y(a,b).
\]
The profile is nondecreasing in \(r\), need not be symmetric in \(F,G\), and may take the value \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An image-excess profile gives, at each domain radius, the largest directed excess of one multifunction’s values over another’s.
knowledge_statements.title: Image-Excess Profiles

source_witnesses.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

children.title: Hausdorff Image Profiles
children.top_down_role: Symmetric Hausdorff measurements across domain-indexed images.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d_X)\) and \((Y,d_Y)\) are metric spaces, with base point \(x_0\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The profile \(H_r(F,G)\) is the pointwise symmetrization of the two directed image-excess profiles.

notation.meaning: Hausdorff distance on nonempty compact subsets of Y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric image profile for compact-valued multifunctions.

source_refs.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(r>0\), define
\[
H_r(F,G)=\sup_{x\in B_X(r)}d_H\bigl(F(x),G(x)\bigr).
\]
Since \(d_H(A,B)=\max\{e_Y(A,B),e_Y(B,A)\}\), one has the exact representation
\[
H_r(F,G)=\max\bigl\{E_r(F\mid G),E_r(G\mid F)\bigr\}.
\]
Thus \(H_r\) is symmetric and nondecreasing in \(r\), and \(H_r(F_n,F)\to0\) expresses uniform Hausdorff convergence on \(B_X(r)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Hausdorff image profile is exactly the maximum of the two oppositely directed image-excess profiles.
knowledge_statements.title: Hausdorff Image Profiles

source_witnesses.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

children.title: Directional-Symmetric Metric Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Relations between one-sided image excess and symmetric image distance.

assumptions_latex: \(F,G:X\to\mathcal K(Y)\), where \(X,Y\) are metric spaces and \(x_0\in X\).
\(E_m(F\mid G)\) and \(H_m(F,G)\) are the radius-\(m\) directed and symmetric image profiles.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The symmetric profile metric lies between the maximum and the sum of its two directional counterparts.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative comparison of integrated directional and symmetric image profiles.

source_refs.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
D^{\to}(F,G)=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}2^{-m}\min\{1,E_m(F\mid G)\},
\qquad
D^H(F,G)=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}2^{-m}\min\{1,H_m(F,G)\}.
\]
Then
\[
\max\{D^{\to}(F,G),D^{\to}(G,F)\}
\le D^H(F,G)
\le D^{\to}(F,G)+D^{\to}(G,F).
\]
Hence convergence in the symmetric profile metric is equivalent to convergence in both directional profile discrepancies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The symmetric image-profile metric is equivalent to requiring both directional excess-profile discrepancies to vanish.
knowledge_statements.title: Directional-Symmetric Metric Comparisons

source_witnesses.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional-Derivative and Subdifferential Upper Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded finite-dimensional result for pointwise convergence on an open convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty] be convex, let C\subset\mathbb{R}^n be open and convex with f finite on C, and let (f_i) be convex functions finite on C such that f_i(u)\to f(u) for every u\in C. If x_i\in C, x_i\to x\in C, and y_i\to y\in\mathbb{R}^n, then \limsup_{i\to\infty}f_i'(x_i;y_i)\le f'(x;y). Moreover, for every \varepsilon>0 there exists i_0 such that \partial f_i(x_i)\subseteq\partial f(x)+\varepsilon B for all i\ge i_0, where B is the Euclidean unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex functions finite on a common open convex set and converging there pointwise, directional derivatives along convergent base points and directions have an upper-limit bounded by the limiting directional derivative. The corresponding subdifferentials are eventually contained in any prescribed Euclidean enlargement of the limiting subdifferential.
assumptions_latex: C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is open and convex, and }f\text{ is finite on }C
f_i\text{ is convex and finite on }C\text{ for every }i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \limsup_{i\to\infty}f_i'(x_i;y_i)\le f'(x;y),\qquad \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists i_0\ \forall i\ge i_0:\ \partial f_i(x_i)\subseteq\partial f(x)+\varepsilon B.

source_evidence.locator: Complete book / 24. Differential Continuity and Monotonicity / Theorem 24.5

source_refs.locator: Complete book / 24. Differential Continuity and Monotonicity / Theorem 24.5

knowledge_statements.title: Directional-Derivative and Subdifferential Upper Limits

source_witnesses.locator: Complete book / 24. Differential Continuity and Monotonicity / Theorem 24.5
