knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stability under pointwise convergence of finite saddle functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise convergence is imposed on a common open convex finiteness region, with base points allowed to vary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K and K_i be concave in u and convex in v, all finite on an open convex set C\times D, with K_i\to K pointwise on C\times D. If (u_i,v_i)\to(u,v) in C\times D, then for every u'\in\mathbb{R}^m and v'\in\mathbb{R}^n, \liminf_{i\to\infty}K_i'(u_i,v_i;u',0)\ge K'(u,v;u',0) and \limsup_{i\to\infty}K_i'(u_i,v_i;0,v')\le K'(u,v;0,v'). Moreover, for every \varepsilon>0 there is i_0 such that \partial K_i(u_i,v_i)\subseteq\partial K(u,v)+\varepsilon B for all i\ge i_0, where B is the Euclidean unit ball in \mathbb{R}^{m+n}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under pointwise convergence on a common open finiteness region and convergence of the base points, first-block directional derivatives satisfy a lower-limit inequality and second-block derivatives satisfy an upper-limit inequality. The moving saddle subdifferentials are eventually contained in every Euclidean enlargement of the limiting subdifferential.
assumptions_latex: K,K_i\text{ are concave in }u\text{ and convex in }v
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall u'\in\mathbb{R}^m,\ \liminf_iK_i'(u_i,v_i;u',0)\ge K'(u,v;u',0);\quad\forall v'\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ \limsup_iK_i'(u_i,v_i;0,v')\le K'(u,v;0,v');\quad\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists i_0\ \forall i\ge i_0,\ \partial K_i(u_i,v_i)\subseteq\partial K(u,v)+\varepsilon B.

source_evidence.locator: Complete book / 35. Continuity and Differentiability of Saddle-Functions / Theorem 35.7

assumptions_latex: \((X,d_X)\) is a metric space and \((Y,d_Y)\) is a metric space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((F_n)\) is equicontinuous exactly when the displayed modulus condition holds uniformly in \(n\).

notation.meaning: Hausdorff distance induced by the metric on Y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hausdorff equicontinuity of a compact-valued multifunction sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sequence \((F_n)\) is equicontinuous at \(x\in X\) if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(\delta>0\), independent of \(n\), such that
\[
d_X(x,x')<\delta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d_H\bigl(F_n(x),F_n(x')\bigr)<\varepsilon
\]
for every \(x'\in X\) and every \(n\). It is equicontinuous on \(X\) when it is equicontinuous at every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equicontinuity requires one local input tolerance to control the Hausdorff variation of every multifunction in the sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Equicontinuity of Multifunction Sequences

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a locally compact, second-countable metric space and \((Y,d_Y)\) is a metric space.
\(F_n:X\to\mathcal K(Y)\) are continuous and form an equicontinuous sequence.
For every \(x\in X\), the set \(\{F_n(x):n\ge1\}\) has compact closure in \((\mathcal K(Y),d_H)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A subsequence converges compact-uniformly in Hausdorff distance to a continuous compact-valued multifunction.

notation.meaning: Hausdorff metric on nonempty compact subsets of Y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential Arzelà–Ascoli theorem in the Hausdorff hyperspace.

source_refs.locator: G. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 175

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exist indices \(n_1<n_2<\cdots\) and a continuous mapping \(F:X\to\mathcal K(Y)\) such that, for every compact set \(K\subset X\),
\[
\sup_{x\in K}d_H\bigl(F_{n_j}(x),F(x)\bigr)\longrightarrow0
\quad\text{as }j\to\infty.
\]
Equivalently, every equicontinuous, pointwise relatively compact sequence of continuous \(\mathcal K(Y)\)-valued mappings is sequentially relatively compact for compact-uniform convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equicontinuity and pointwise relative compactness yield a subsequence converging uniformly on compact sets to a continuous compact-valued multifunction.
knowledge_statements.title: Arzelà–Ascoli-Type Multifunction Compactness

source_witnesses.locator: G. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 175

children.title: Generic Continuity Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Convergence consequences involving residual or generic continuity behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Baire metric space and \(Y\) is a compact metric space.
\(F:X\to\mathcal K(Y)\) is Baire-one for the Hausdorff metric on nonempty compact subsets of \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in X:F\text{ is Hausdorff-continuous at }x\}\) is residual in \(X\).

notation.meaning: Hausdorff distance induced by the metric of Y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Baire-one compact-valued version of generic continuity.

source_refs.locator: J.* Generic Continuity and Selections p. 187

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Baire metric space, let \(Y\) be a compact metric space, and equip \(\mathcal K(Y)\) with the Hausdorff metric \(d_H\). If \(F:X\to\mathcal K(Y)\) is the pointwise Hausdorff limit of continuous mappings \(F_k:X\to\mathcal K(Y)\), then the set of points \(x\in X\) at which \(d_H(F(x'),F(x))\to0\) whenever \(x'\to x\) is a dense \(G_\delta\) subset of \(X\). Thus a Baire-one compact-valued multifunction admits a residual interface on which ordinary sequential limits and value-set limits agree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact-valued multifunction that is a pointwise limit of continuous multifunctions is Hausdorff-continuous on a residual set of its Baire domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Generic Continuity Interfaces

source_witnesses.locator: J.* Generic Continuity and Selections p. 187

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interior Upper Semicontinuity of Directional Derivatives and Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded local continuity result for a proper convex function on the interior of its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty] is proper and convex, then (x,y)\mapsto f'(x;y) is upper semicontinuous on \operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\times\mathbb{R}^n. Moreover, for every x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f) and every \varepsilon>0, there exists \delta>0 such that \partial f(z)\subseteq\partial f(x)+\varepsilon B for every z\in x+\delta B, where B is the Euclidean unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper convex function, the directional derivative is jointly upper semicontinuous in the base point and direction when the base point lies in the interior of the effective domain. Nearby subdifferentials are contained in any prescribed enlargement of the subdifferential at an interior point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x,y)\mapsto f'(x;y)\text{ is upper semicontinuous on }\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\times\mathbb{R}^n,\quad \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists\delta>0\ \forall z\in x+\delta B:\ \partial f(z)\subseteq\partial f(x)+\varepsilon B.

children.title: Selection-Limit Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Limit behavior of selected trajectories or selected single-valued representatives.

assumptions_latex: Graph convergence means Painlevé-Kuratowski convergence in \(X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}F_n\to\operatorname{gph}F\) exactly when the outer and inner selection conditions both hold.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential characterization of graphical convergence in metric spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The graphical convergence \(\operatorname{gph}F_n\to\operatorname{gph}F\) is equivalent to the following two selection-limit interfaces. First, whenever \(n_k\uparrow\infty\), \(x_k\to x\), \(y_k\to y\), and \(y_k\in F_{n_k}(x_k)\), one has \(y\in F(x)\). Second, for every \(x\in X\) and \(y\in F(x)\), there exist \(x_n\to x\) and \(y_n\to y\) such that \(y_n\in F_n(x_n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). The first condition controls all convergent selected subsequences, while the second supplies recovery selections for every limiting graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graphical convergence is equivalent to an outer closedness rule for convergent selections plus a recovery-selection rule for every point of the limiting graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Selection-Limit Interfaces

children.title: Selection-Theory Boundary
children.top_down_role: Boundary between convergence questions retained here and selection theory owned elsewhere.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is paracompact, \(E\) is a Banach space, and \(F:X\rightrightarrows E\) is lower semicontinuous.
The values of \(F\) are nonempty and closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convexity guarantees a continuous selection, whereas closed nonconvex values need not do so.

notation.meaning: Unit circle in the complex plane
Square-root multifunction on the unit circle

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-valued continuous-selection boundary with a circle counterexample.

source_refs.locator: J.* Generic Continuity and Selections p. 187

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every value \(F(x)\) is convex, then the lower semicontinuous multifunction \(F:X\rightrightarrows E\) has a continuous selection \(f:X\to E\) satisfying \(f(x)\in F(x)\) for every \(x\in X\). Closedness without convexity is insufficient: the compact-valued multifunction \(R:\mathbb S^1\rightrightarrows\mathbb S^1\), defined by \(R(z)=\{w\in\mathbb S^1:w^2=z\}\), is continuous and has nonempty finite closed values but has no continuous selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower semicontinuous multifunction with nonempty closed convex values has a continuous selection, while closed nonconvex values do not suffice, as shown by the square-root multifunction on the circle.
knowledge_statements.title: Selection-Theory Boundary

source_witnesses.locator: J.* Generic Continuity and Selections p. 187

children.title: Inverse-Multifunction Limits
children.top_down_role: Convergence behavior under inversion of set-valued mappings.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_n^{-1}\to F^{-1}\) graphically in \(Y\times X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graphical limits under inversion of a multifunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(n\), define \(F_n^{-1}:Y\rightrightarrows X\) by \(F_n^{-1}(y)=\{x\in X:y\in F_n(x)\}\), and define \(F^{-1}\) analogously. If \(F_n\to F\) graphically in \(X\times Y\), then \(F_n^{-1}\to F^{-1}\) graphically in \(Y\times X\). This limit rule requires no local boundedness or compactness hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graphical convergence is preserved by multifunction inversion, with no additional boundedness or compactness hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Multifunction Limits

children.title: Transposed-Graph Limits
children.top_down_role: Convergence behavior under coordinate transposition of graphs.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are metric spaces and \(C_n,C\subset X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_n^{\mathsf T}\to C^{\mathsf T}\) in \(Y\times X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set convergence under transposition of graph coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a relation \(C\subset X\times Y\), define \(C^{\mathsf T}=\{(y,x)\in Y\times X:(x,y)\in C\}\). If \(C_n\to C\) in the Painleve-Kuratowski sense, then \(C_n^{\mathsf T}\to C^{\mathsf T}\). Transposition commutes with both the outer and inner set limits and requires no auxiliary compactness hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transposing each relation by swapping its coordinates preserves Painleve-Kuratowski convergence without an additional compactness hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.title: Transposed-Graph Limits

children.title: Inversion–Transposition Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The convergence interface linking inverse mappings with transposed graphs.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}(F^{-1})=(\operatorname{gph}F)^{\mathsf T}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact identification of inversion with graph transposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every multifunction \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), define \(F^{-1}:Y\rightrightarrows X\) by \(x\in F^{-1}(y)\) if and only if \(y\in F(x)\). Its graph representation is
\[\operatorname{gph}(F^{-1})=\{(y,x):(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\}=(\operatorname{gph}F)^{\mathsf T}.\]
Both operations are involutive: \((F^{-1})^{-1}=F\) and \(((\operatorname{gph}F)^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T}=\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multifunction inversion is represented exactly by graph transposition, and both operations are involutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Inversion–Transposition Correspondence

children.title: Multifunction Sum Limits
children.top_down_role: Convergence behavior of pointwise set-valued sums.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is metric and \(Y\) is a finite-dimensional normed space.
The sets \(H_n(x')\) are locally uniformly bounded near each \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_n+G_n\to F+G\) graphically.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional sum rule using joint graphical convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H_n:X\rightrightarrows Y\times Y\) be given by \(H_n(x)=F_n(x)\times G_n(x)\), and suppose \(H_n\to H\) graphically with \(H(x)=F(x)\times G(x)\). Assume that for every \(x\in X\) there are a neighborhood \(U\) of \(x\), a bounded set \(B\subset Y\times Y\), and \(n_0\) such that \(H_n(x')\subset B\) for \(x'\in U\) and \(n\ge n_0\). Then the continuous addition map \(a(y,z)=y+z\) yields graphical convergence \(a\circ H_n\to a\circ H\), equivalently \(F_n+G_n\to F+G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint graphical convergence of the two summands, together with local uniform boundedness, passes through addition and yields convergence of their pointwise sums.
knowledge_statements.title: Multifunction Sum Limits

children.title: Multifunction Product Limits
children.top_down_role: Convergence behavior of product-valued mapping constructions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is metric, \(Y_1,Y_2,Z\) are finite-dimensional normed spaces, and \(b:Y_1\times Y_2\to Z\) is continuous bilinear.
The joint values are locally uniformly bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b(F_n,G_n)\to b(F,G)\) graphically.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous bilinear-product rule with bounded joint factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(H_n(x)=F_n(x)\times G_n(x)\) and \(H(x)=F(x)\times G(x)\). Suppose \(H_n\to H\) graphically and, locally in \(x\), all sufficiently late values of \(H_n\) lie in one bounded subset of \(Y_1\times Y_2\). For the multifunction \(P_n:X\rightrightarrows Z\) defined by \(P_n(x)=\{b(y,z):y\in F_n(x),\ z\in G_n(x)\}\), one then has \(P_n\to P\) graphically, where \(P(x)=\{b(y,z):y\in F(x),\ z\in G(x)\}\). The boundedness prevents factor pairs with finite products from escaping to infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous bilinear operation preserves joint graphical convergence when the factor pairs are locally uniformly bounded, preventing hidden products from escaping factors.
knowledge_statements.title: Multifunction Product Limits

children.title: Cartesian-Construction Limits
children.top_down_role: Convergence behavior of Cartesian products of values or graphs.

assumptions_latex: \(F_n:X_1\rightrightarrows Y_1\) and \(G_n:X_2\rightrightarrows Y_2\) converge graphically to \(F\) and \(G\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_n\boxtimes G_n\to F\boxtimes G\) graphically.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite Cartesian products of independently convergent graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \((F_n\boxtimes G_n)(x_1,x_2)=F_n(x_1)\times G_n(x_2)\) and define \(F\boxtimes G\) analogously. If \(F_n\to F\) and \(G_n\to G\) graphically, then \(F_n\boxtimes G_n\to F\boxtimes G\) graphically. Under the canonical regrouping of coordinates,
\[\operatorname{gph}(F_n\boxtimes G_n)=\operatorname{gph}F_n\times\operatorname{gph}G_n.\]
No compactness assumption is required for this finite independent Cartesian construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite Cartesian products of independently graph-convergent multifunctions converge graphically, with no additional compactness assumption.
knowledge_statements.title: Cartesian-Construction Limits

children.title: Product-Compactness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Compactness restrictions affecting product and Cartesian limit preservation.

assumptions_latex: Set convergence is Painleve-Kuratowski convergence in Euclidean spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without bounded factor pairs, convergence of sets need not pass to their product images.

notation.meaning: A sequence of two-point factor sets

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Escaping-factor obstruction for product-image convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb R^2\), let \(A_n=\{(n,1/n),(0,1)\}\) and \(A=\{(0,1)\}\). Then \(A_n\to A\) in the Painleve-Kuratowski sense. For the continuous multiplication map \(m:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\), one has \(m(A_n)=\{0,1\}\) for every \(n\), while \(m(A)=\{0\}\). Thus \(m(A_n)\) does not converge to \(m(A)\), exhibiting failure of product-image convergence when factor pairs may escape to infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sets consisting of an escaping factor pair and a fixed pair converge, but their multiplication images do not, demonstrating the need to control unbounded factor pairs.
knowledge_statements.title: Product-Compactness Boundaries

children.title: Direct Composition Limits
children.top_down_role: Convergence of ordinary compositions of set-valued mappings.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y,Z\) are finite-dimensional normed spaces and \(F_n:X\rightrightarrows Y\), \(G_n:Y\rightrightarrows Z\) converge graphically to \(F\) and \(G\), respectively.
Whenever \(n_k\uparrow\infty\), \(x_k\to x\), \(z_k\to z\), and \(z_k\in(G_{n_k}\circ F_{n_k})(x_k)\), there are bounded witnesses \(y_k\in F_{n_k}(x_k)\) satisfying \(z_k\in G_{n_k}(y_k)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\limsup_n\operatorname{gph}(G_n\circ F_n)\subset\operatorname{gph}(G\circ F)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer-limit theorem for compositions with bounded intermediate witnesses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H_n=G_n\circ F_n\) and \(H=G\circ F\). Assume that whenever \(n_k\uparrow\infty\), \(x_k\to x\), \(z_k\to z\), and \(z_k\in H_{n_k}(x_k)\), there exist witnesses \(y_k\in F_{n_k}(x_k)\) such that \(z_k\in G_{n_k}(y_k)\) and the sequence \((y_k)\) is bounded. Then
\[\limsup_n\operatorname{gph}H_n\subset\operatorname{gph}H.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every convergent outer sequence for the compositions has a bounded choice of intermediate witnesses, graphical convergence of the component multifunctions yields the outer graphical limit inclusion for their compositions.
knowledge_statements.title: Direct Composition Limits

children.title: Implicit Composition Limits
children.top_down_role: Convergence of compositions mediated by latent variables or relational constraints.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y,Z\) are metric spaces and \(F_n:X\rightrightarrows Y\), \(G_n:Y\rightrightarrows Z\).
Every \((x,z)\in\operatorname{gph}(G\circ F)\) admits a witness \(y\in F(x)\) with \(z\in G(y)\) and a compatible recovery sequence through \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}(G\circ F)\subset\liminf_n\operatorname{gph}(G_n\circ F_n)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatible-lifting condition for the inner composition limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H_n=G_n\circ F_n\) and \(H=G\circ F\). A compatible-lifting condition is that, for every \(x\in X\) and \(z\in H(x)\), there exist \(y\in F(x)\) with \(z\in G(y)\) and sequences \(x_n\to x\), \(y_n\to y\), and \(z_n\to z\) such that \(y_n\in F_n(x_n)\) and \(z_n\in G_n(y_n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). Under this condition,
\[\operatorname{gph}H\subset\liminf_n\operatorname{gph}H_n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inner composition limit follows when every point of the limiting composition graph has one intermediate witness admitting compatible recovery sequences through both component multifunctions.
knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Composition Limits

children.title: Intermediate-Variable Compactness
children.top_down_role: Compactness requirements for variables eliminated during composition.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y,Z\) are metric spaces and \(F_n:X\rightrightarrows Y\), \(G_n:Y\rightrightarrows Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\limsup_n\operatorname{gph}(G_n\circ F_n)\subset\operatorname{gph}(G\circ F)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential compactness condition supporting the outer-limit calculus for compositions of multifunctions.

source_refs.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that whenever \(x_{n_k}\to x\), \(z_{n_k}\to z\), and \(z_{n_k}\in(G_{n_k}\circ F_{n_k})(x_{n_k})\), there exist intermediate points \(y_k\in F_{n_k}(x_{n_k})\) with \(z_{n_k}\in G_{n_k}(y_k)\) such that \((y_k)\) has a convergent subsequence. Then every outer graphical cluster point \((x,z)\) of the compositions has an intermediate point \(y\) satisfying \(y\in F(x)\) and \(z\in G(y)\). Consequently, \[\limsup_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{gph}(G_n\circ F_n)\subset\operatorname{gph}(G\circ F).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer graphical limits pass through composition when every convergent input-output sequence admits a subsequentially convergent sequence of intermediate variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Intermediate-Variable Compactness

source_witnesses.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

children.title: Qualification Failures
children.top_down_role: Limit mismatches caused by missing compatibility or regularity conditions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_n\cap B_n=\varnothing\) for every \(n\), although \(A_n\to B\) and \(B_n\to B\) with \(B\cap B=B\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary intersection counterregime illustrating why operation qualifications cannot be omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_n=\mathbb R\times\{1/n\}\), \(B_n=B=\mathbb R\times\{0\}\), and use Painleve-Kuratowski convergence. Then \(A_n\to B\) and \(B_n\to B\), but \(A_n\cap B_n=\varnothing\) for every \(n\). Hence \[\lim_{n\to\infty}(A_n\cap B_n)=\varnothing\ne B=(\lim_{n\to\infty}A_n)\cap(\lim_{n\to\infty}B_n).\] Thus convergence of the operands alone does not justify passing a limit through intersection; a qualification preventing asymptotically incompatible contact is essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two convergent set sequences can have empty intersections even though their limits coincide, so intersection calculus requires an additional qualification.
knowledge_statements.title: Qualification Failures

children.title: Compactness Failures
children.top_down_role: Limit mismatches caused by escaping or nonprecompact intermediate objects.

assumptions_latex: \(F_n,G_n:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\) are the multifunctions specified below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}F_n\to\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{gph}G_n\to\varnothing\), while \(\operatorname{gph}(G_n\circ F_n)=\{(0,0)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Escaping intermediate variables destroy the expected outer-limit inclusion for composition.

source_refs.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(F_n(0)=\{n\}\), \(F_n(x)=\varnothing\) for \(x\ne0\), and \(G_n(n)=\{0\}\), \(G_n(y)=\varnothing\) for \(y\ne n\). Both graphs escape every bounded region, so \(\operatorname{gph}F_n\to\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{gph}G_n\to\varnothing\) in the Painleve-Kuratowski sense. Nevertheless, \[(G_n\circ F_n)(0)=\{0\},\qquad \operatorname{gph}(G_n\circ F_n)=\{(0,0)\}.\] The composition retains a finite limit point solely through the unbounded intermediate variable \(n\), demonstrating failure without intermediate-variable compactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Component graphs may escape while their compositions retain finite points because unbounded intermediate variables cancel the escape.
knowledge_statements.title: Compactness Failures

source_witnesses.locator: E. Pointwise and Graphical Convergence p. 166

children.title: Operation-Specific Counterregimes
children.top_down_role: Failure patterns specific to inversion, products, sums, or composition.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_n\to\varnothing\) and \(B_n\to\varnothing\), but \(A_n+B_n=\{0\}\) for every \(n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minkowski addition has an escape-cancellation counterregime distinct from intersection and composition failures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_n=\{n\}\) and \(B_n=\{-n\}\). In \(\mathbb R\), both sequences converge in the Painleve-Kuratowski sense to the empty set because their unique points escape to infinity. However, their Minkowski sums satisfy \[A_n+B_n=\{n-n\}=\{0\}\quad\text{for every }n.\] Hence \(A_n+B_n\to\{0\}\), whereas the sum of the operand limits is empty. This operation-specific failure is caused by cancellation between two unbounded selections and is excluded by suitable boundedness or no-cancellation hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minkowski sums can retain finite points through cancellation of unbounded operands even when both operand sequences converge to the empty set.
knowledge_statements.title: Operation-Specific Counterregimes

children.title: Variational Convergence of Functions
children.top_down_role: Function convergence encoded by epigraphs, topological approximation, minimization behavior, and mixed strong–weak geometries.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Variational Convergence for Functions and Operators
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Variational Convergence for Functions and Operators

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space and \(f_n,f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n\xrightarrow{e}f\) exactly when \(\operatorname{epi}f_n\to\operatorname{epi}f\) in \(X\times\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-limit definition of epigraphical convergence on a metric space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), define its epigraph by \[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,r)\in X\times\mathbb R:f(x)\le r\}.\] The sequence \((f_n)\) converges epigraphically to \(f\), written \(f_n\xrightarrow{e}f\), when the epigraphs converge in the Painleve-Kuratowski sense in the product metric space: \[\liminf_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{epi}f_n=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{epi}f_n=\operatorname{epi}f.\] Equivalently, the lower and upper set limits of the epigraphs agree with the epigraph of the limiting function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epigraphical convergence is precisely Painleve-Kuratowski convergence of the functions' epigraphs in the product space.
knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Set Limits

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space and \(f_n,f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n\xrightarrow{h}f\) exactly when \(\operatorname{hypo}f_n\to\operatorname{hypo}f\) in \(X\times\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-limit definition of hypographical convergence on a metric space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), define its hypograph by \[\operatorname{hypo}f=\{(x,r)\in X\times\mathbb R:r\le f(x)\}.\] The sequence \((f_n)\) converges hypographically to \(f\), written \(f_n\xrightarrow{h}f\), when \[\liminf_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{hypo}f_n=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{hypo}f_n=\operatorname{hypo}f.\] Equivalently, hypographical convergence of \((f_n)\) is epigraphical convergence of \((-f_n)\) to \(-f\), with the usual extended-real sign convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hypographical convergence is Painleve-Kuratowski convergence of hypographs, equivalently epigraphical convergence after negating the functions.
knowledge_statements.title: Hypograph Set Limits

children.title: Level-Set Convergence
children.top_down_role: Set convergence of fixed-value level sets.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space, \(f_n,f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_\alpha(f_n)\to L_\alpha(f)\) is level-set convergence at \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-level convergence at one fixed finite threshold.

source_refs.locator: C. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 250

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the level set of \(f\) at \(\alpha\) by \[L_\alpha(f)=\{x\in X:f(x)=\alpha\}.\] The sequence \((f_n)\) has level-set convergence to \(f\) at \(\alpha\) when \[\liminf_{n\to\infty}L_\alpha(f_n)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}L_\alpha(f_n)=L_\alpha(f).\] In sequential terms, every limit of points \(x_{n_k}\in L_\alpha(f_{n_k})\) belongs to \(L_\alpha(f)\), and each \(x\in L_\alpha(f)\) is approached by some sequence \(x_n\in L_\alpha(f_n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Level-set convergence means that the exact equality sets at a fixed threshold converge in the Painleve-Kuratowski sense.
knowledge_statements.title: Level-Set Convergence

source_witnesses.locator: C. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 250

children.title: Sublevel-Set Convergence
children.top_down_role: Set convergence of threshold-indexed sublevel sets.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space, \(f_n,f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_\alpha(f_n)\to S_\alpha(f)\) is sublevel-set convergence at \(\alpha\).

notation.meaning: closed sublevel set at threshold alpha

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-sublevel convergence at one fixed finite threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the closed sublevel set of \(f\) at \(\alpha\) by \[S_\alpha(f)=\{x\in X:f(x)\le\alpha\}.\] The sequence \((f_n)\) has sublevel-set convergence to \(f\) at \(\alpha\) when \[\liminf_{n\to\infty}S_\alpha(f_n)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}S_\alpha(f_n)=S_\alpha(f).\] Thus every cluster point of points satisfying \(f_n(x_n)\le\alpha\) must satisfy \(f(x)\le\alpha\), and every point of \(S_\alpha(f)\) must admit approximating points in the corresponding sublevel sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sublevel-set convergence is Painleve-Kuratowski convergence of the sets on which each function does not exceed a fixed threshold.
knowledge_statements.title: Sublevel-Set Convergence

children.title: Threshold-Exceptional Regimes
children.top_down_role: Threshold values where set-limit representations change or cease to agree.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space and \(f_n\xrightarrow{e}f\), where \(f_n,f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{\{f<\alpha\}}\subset\liminf_n S_\alpha(f_n)\subset\limsup_n S_\alpha(f_n)\subset\{f\le\alpha\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold regularity boundary for deriving sublevel convergence from epigraphical convergence.

source_refs.locator: C. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 250

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite threshold \(\alpha\), epigraphical convergence yields the sandwich \[\overline{\{x:f(x)<\alpha\}}\subset\liminf_{n\to\infty}S_\alpha(f_n)\subset\limsup_{n\to\infty}S_\alpha(f_n)\subset\{x:f(x)\le\alpha\}.\] Therefore, if \(\overline{\{f<\alpha\}}=\{f\le\alpha\}\), then \(S_\alpha(f_n)\to S_\alpha(f)\). Thresholds for which this density equality fails are exceptional: epigraphical convergence alone need not recover boundary points lying in \(\{f=\alpha\}\) but outside \(\overline{\{f<\alpha\}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epi-convergence gives sublevel convergence at thresholds where strict sublevels are dense in closed sublevels; failure of this density identifies exceptional thresholds.
knowledge_statements.title: Threshold-Exceptional Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: C. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 250

children.title: Pointwise Comparison Regimes
children.top_down_role: Interfaces between pointwise convergence and stronger or variational modes.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb R\) and \(f_n:X\to\mathbb R\) is defined below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n\to1\) pointwise, but \(f_n\xrightarrow{e}g\ne1\), where \(g(0)=0\) and \(g(x)=1\) for \(x\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison counterexample separating pointwise and epigraphical limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f_n(1/n)=0\) and \(f_n(x)=1\) for \(x\ne1/n\). For every fixed \(x\in\mathbb R\), one has \(f_n(x)\to1\). Nevertheless, the moving sequence \(x_n=1/n\to0\) satisfies \(f_n(x_n)=0\). In fact, \((f_n)\) converges epigraphically to \(g\) given by \[g(0)=0,\qquad g(x)=1\ \text{for }x\ne0.\] Thus its pointwise limit is the constant function \(1\), while its epigraphical limit is \(g\); neither convergence mode determines the same limit without additional regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A moving narrow dip is invisible pointwise but persists epigraphically, so pointwise and epigraphical convergence can select different limits.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Comparison Regimes

children.title: Continuous-Convergence Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Interfaces involving continuous convergence of functions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space and \(f_n,f:X\to\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n\) converges continuously to \(f\) if and only if \(f_n\xrightarrow{e}f\) and \(f_n\xrightarrow{h}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential continuous convergence compared with simultaneous epi- and hypographical convergence for finite-valued functions.

source_refs.locator: C. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 250

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Continuous convergence means that for every \(x\in X\) and every sequence \(x_n\to x\), \[f_n(x_n)\to f(x).\] This holds if and only if \((f_n)\) converges both epigraphically and hypographically to the same finite-valued function \(f\): \[f_n\xrightarrow{e}f\quad\text{and}\quad f_n\xrightarrow{h}f.\] The epigraphical limit supplies the lower inequality along every moving sequence, while the hypographical limit supplies the upper inequality. In particular, continuous convergence implies pointwise convergence and forces \(f\) to be continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finite-valued functions, continuous convergence is equivalent to simultaneous epigraphical and hypographical convergence to the same limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuous-Convergence Comparisons

source_witnesses.locator: C. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 250

children.title: Uniform-Convergence Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Interfaces involving global or localized uniform convergence.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a compact metric space, \(f_n:X\to\mathbb R\), and \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{x\in X}|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0\) if and only if \(f_n\) converges continuously to \(f\).

notation.meaning: uniform norm of a real-valued function

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact-domain equivalence between uniform convergence to a continuous limit and continuous convergence.

source_refs.locator: C. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 250

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a compact metric space, let \(f_n:X\to\mathbb R\), and let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. Then \[\sup_{x\in X}|f_n(x)-f(x)|\longrightarrow0\] if and only if, for every \(x\in X\) and every sequence \(x_n\to x\), \[f_n(x_n)\longrightarrow f(x).\] Under either condition, \((f_n)\) converges pointwise, epigraphically, and hypographically to \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a compact metric space, uniform convergence to a continuous real-valued limit is equivalent to continuous convergence; either mode also implies pointwise, epigraphical, and hypographical convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform-Convergence Comparisons

source_witnesses.locator: C. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 250

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous convergence implies epi-convergence; in particular, uniform convergence to a finite continuous function implies epi-convergence.

children.title: Epi-Convergence
children.top_down_role: Epigraphical convergence for extended-real-valued functions in the variational-analysis setting.

children.title: Sequential Epi-Convergence
children.top_down_role: Sequence-based descriptions of epigraphical convergence.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{epi}}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential characterization for extended-real functions on a metric space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence \((f_n)\) epi-converges sequentially to \(f\) if, for every \(x\in X\), the following two conditions hold: for every sequence \(x_n\to x\), \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n(x_n)\ge f(x)\); and there exists a sequence \(x_n\to x\) such that \(\limsup_{n\to\infty}f_n(x_n)\le f(x)\). A sequence in the second condition is called a recovery sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential epi-convergence consists of a liminf inequality along every convergent sequence and the existence of a recovery sequence at every point.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Epi-Convergence

children.title: Metric Epi-Convergence
children.top_down_role: Metric descriptions of convergence between epigraphs.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a proper metric space with base point \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_{\mathrm{AW}}(\operatorname{epi}f_n,\operatorname{epi}f)\to0\).

notation.meaning: Attouch–Wets metric on nonempty closed subsets of \(X\times\mathbb R\)
closed product-space ball of radius \(r\) about \((x_0,0)\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attouch–Wets metrization using bounded distance-function comparison.

source_refs.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181; Chapter 7. Epigraphical Limits p. 238

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty closed sets \(A,B\subset X\times\mathbb R\), define \[d_{\mathrm{AW}}(A,B)=\int_0^\infty e^{-r}\min\!\left\{1,\sup_{z\in B_r}\left|D(z,A)-D(z,B)\right|\right\}\,dr.\] Metric epi-convergence of \(f_n\) to \(f\) means \(d_{\mathrm{AW}}(\operatorname{epi}f_n,\operatorname{epi}f)\to0\). Positive integrable weights with full support, or corresponding discrete-radius formulas, may be used to define equivalent metrics for the same topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric epi-convergence is Attouch–Wets convergence of nonempty closed epigraphs, measured by comparing their distance functions on bounded product-space balls.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Epi-Convergence

source_witnesses.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181; Chapter 7. Epigraphical Limits p. 238

children.title: Sequential–Metric Equivalence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Topological settings where sequential and metric descriptions coincide.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{epi}}f\iff d_{\mathrm{AW}}(\operatorname{epi}f_n,\operatorname{epi}f)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence for closed epigraphs in a proper metric setting.

source_refs.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181; B. Epi-Convergence p. 240

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated assumptions, sequential epi-convergence is equivalent to Attouch–Wets convergence of epigraphs. Explicitly, \(f_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{epi}}f\) if and only if \(d_{\mathrm{AW}}(\operatorname{epi}f_n,\operatorname{epi}f)\to0\). Equivalently, the distance functions \(d(\cdot,\operatorname{epi}f_n)\) converge uniformly to \(d(\cdot,\operatorname{epi}f)\) on every bounded subset of \(X\times\mathbb R\). Properness ensures that sequential Painlevé–Kuratowski convergence of the closed epigraphs is captured by this bounded-distance metrization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For closed epigraphs in a proper metric space, sequential epi-convergence and Attouch–Wets metric convergence are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential–Metric Equivalence Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181; B. Epi-Convergence p. 240

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}f_i\to\operatorname{epi}f\) in the Painlevé–Kuratowski sense.

notation.meaning: topological lower and upper set limits

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Net-based epigraph convergence for general topological spaces.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108; Chapter 7. Epigraphical Limits p. 238

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The net \((f_i)\) topologically epi-converges to \(f\) when its epigraphs converge as subsets of \(X\times\mathbb R\): \[\operatorname{Li}_i\operatorname{epi}f_i=\operatorname{epi}f=\operatorname{Ls}_i\operatorname{epi}f_i.\] Equivalently, every convergent subnet of points \((x_i,\alpha_i)\in\operatorname{epi}f_i\) has its limit in \(\operatorname{epi}f\), and every \((x,\alpha)\in\operatorname{epi}f\) is the limit of a suitable subnet of epigraph points. In first-countable spaces these conditions admit sequential formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Topological epi-convergence is Painlevé–Kuratowski convergence of epigraphs, formulated with nets in a general topological space.
knowledge_statements.title: Topological Epi-Convergence

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Set Convergence p. 108; Chapter 7. Epigraphical Limits p. 238

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited Rockafellar–Wets sections do not by themselves establish the proposed arbitrary-topological-space, net-based formulation. The claimed subnet characterization is also underspecified because epigraph points come from varying sets and the relevant inner-limit net need not be a subnet of the original index net. An authoritative general-topology source and precise definitions of the set limits are required.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n\) converges totally epigraphically to \(f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Provisional bounded-Hausdorff interpretation; terminology requires source confirmation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the provisional bounded-Hausdorff convention, \((f_n)\) converges totally epigraphically to \(f\) when, for every radius \(r>0\) at which truncation is stable, \[d_H\!\left(\operatorname{epi}f_n\cap B_r,\operatorname{epi}f\cap B_r\right)\to0.\] Here empty truncations require an explicit extended-distance convention. This mode controls the entire epigraph through all bounded windows and is stronger than unquantified local hit-and-miss convergence unless compactness or properness makes the formulations equivalent. The precise meaning of “total epi-convergence” varies across sources and must be fixed before promotion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Provisionally, total epi-convergence means Hausdorff convergence of epigraphs in every bounded window; the project’s intended terminology needs source confirmation.
knowledge_statements.title: Total Epi-Convergence

The mathematical definition cannot be fixed reliably without a source that identifies the intended terminology.

children.title: Epi-Distance Families
children.top_down_role: Distance constructions for epigraphs or extended-real-valued functions.

assumptions_latex: \((Z,\rho)\) is a metric space with base point \(z_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_{\mathrm{AW}}(A,B)=0\iff A=B\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-function and integrated localization family for closed sets.

source_refs.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\delta_r(A,B)=\sup_{z\in B_r}|\rho(z,A)-\rho(z,B)|\] and \[d_{\mathrm{AW}}(A,B)=\int_0^\infty e^{-r}\min\{1,\delta_r(A,B)\}\,dr.\] Each \(\delta_r\) quantifies discrepancy visible inside radius \(r\), while the integral combines all scales into a finite metric. Replacing the integral by \(\sum_{k\ge1}2^{-k}\min\{1,\delta_k(A,B)\}\) yields an equivalent metric. Applied to \(A=\operatorname{epi}f\) and \(B=\operatorname{epi}g\), these form epi-distance families.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Localized distance-function discrepancies, combined by an integral or weighted series, define equivalent Attouch–Wets epi-distance families.
knowledge_statements.title: Epi-Distance Families

source_witnesses.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

children.title: Quantified Epigraphical Limits
children.top_down_role: Rate-sensitive or error-sensitive descriptions of epigraphical convergence.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{epi}}f\iff \delta_r(\operatorname{epi}f_n,\operatorname{epi}f)\to0\) for every \(r>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantified bounded-distance characterization in proper metric spaces.

source_refs.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181; B. Epi-Convergence p. 240

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(r>0\), let \(B_r\) be the product-space ball about a fixed base point and define \[\delta_r(\operatorname{epi}f_n,\operatorname{epi}f)=\sup_{z\in B_r}\left|d(z,\operatorname{epi}f_n)-d(z,\operatorname{epi}f)\right|.\] Then \(f_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{epi}}f\) if and only if \(\delta_r(\operatorname{epi}f_n,\operatorname{epi}f)\to0\) for every finite \(r\). Equivalently, any Attouch–Wets metric assembled from these localized discrepancies tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epi-convergence of closed epigraphs is equivalent to uniform convergence of their distance functions on every bounded region.
knowledge_statements.title: Quantified Epigraphical Limits

source_witnesses.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181; B. Epi-Convergence p. 240

children.title: Localization by Truncation
children.top_down_role: Quantitative epigraph comparisons restricted by bounded regions or scales.

assumptions_latex: \((Z,\rho)\) is a metric space with base point \(z_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_{\mathrm{AW}}(A,B)\) is determined by the family \((\delta_r(A,B))_{r>0}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Localization through bounded distance-function truncations, avoiding boundary artifacts.

source_refs.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Localization is performed by restricting distance functions, not merely the sets: \[\delta_r(A,B)=\sup_{z\in B_r}|\rho(z,A)-\rho(z,B)|.\] Thus points of \(A\) or \(B\) outside \(B_r\) may still influence distances measured inside \(B_r\), preventing artificial errors caused by cutting sets at the boundary. The family is monotone in \(r\), and convergence \(\delta_r(A_n,A)\to0\) for every \(r>0\) is equivalent to convergence in any weighted integral or discrete Attouch–Wets metric built from these truncations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Localize closed sets by comparing their distance functions on bounded balls; this avoids the boundary artifacts of directly intersecting sets with balls.
knowledge_statements.title: Localization by Truncation

source_witnesses.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

children.title: Algebraic Function Operations
children.top_down_role: Epi-limit behavior under sums, scalar actions, maxima, or related algebraic constructions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n+g_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{epi}}f+g\) and \(a_nf_n+c_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{epi}}af+c\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stable addition and positive affine scaling under continuous perturbations.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 7. Epigraphical Limits p. 238; B. Epi-Convergence p. 240

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated assumptions, \(f_n+g_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{epi}}f+g\) and \(a_nf_n+c_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{epi}}af+c\). Addition of two sequences that are only known to epi-converge is not covered without an additional compatibility condition, such as the existence of common recovery sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epi-convergence is preserved by continuously convergent finite additive perturbations and by convergent positive affine rescaling; sums of two merely epi-convergent sequences require an additional compatibility condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic Function Operations

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 7. Epigraphical Limits p. 238; B. Epi-Convergence p. 240

children.title: Composite Function Operations
children.top_down_role: Epi-limit behavior under composition with mappings or outer functions.

assumptions_latex: \(\phi:\overline{\mathbb R}\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is continuous in the order topology and strictly increasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi\circ f_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{epi}}\phi\circ f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer scalar composition by a continuous strictly increasing transformation of the extended real line.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 7. Epigraphical Limits p. 238; B. Epi-Convergence p. 240

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated assumptions, \(\phi\circ f_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{epi}}\phi\circ f\). A decreasing or discontinuous outer map need not preserve epi-convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous strictly increasing transformations of the extended real line preserve epi-convergence; decreasing or discontinuous outer transformations need not do so.
knowledge_statements.title: Composite Function Operations

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 7. Epigraphical Limits p. 238; B. Epi-Convergence p. 240

children.title: Algebraic Qualification Regimes
children.top_down_role: Compatibility conditions governing preservation under algebraic operations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n+g_n\xrightarrow{e}f+g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A common-recovery qualification for epi-convergence of sums without indeterminate extended-real addition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that for every \(x\in X\) with \(f(x)+g(x)<+\infty\), there exists a sequence \(x_n\to x\) such that \(f_n(x_n)\to f(x)\) and \(g_n(x_n)\to g(x)\). Then \(f_n+g_n\xrightarrow{e}f+g\). A sufficient specialization is that \(g_n\to g\) locally uniformly, \(g\) is finite and continuous, and \(f_n\xrightarrow{e}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epi-convergent summands that never take minus infinity have an epi-convergent sum when every finite limit point admits one recovery sequence for both summands.
knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic Qualification Regimes

children.title: Composition Qualification Regimes
children.top_down_role: Compatibility conditions governing preservation under composite constructions.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are metric spaces, \(G_n:X\to Y\), and \(h_n:Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h_n\circ G_n\xrightarrow{e}h\circ G\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A recovery-lifting qualification for composition under varying maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume additionally that for every \(x\in X\) with \(h(G(x))<+\infty\), some sequence \(x_n\to x\) satisfies \(h_n(G_n(x_n))\to h(G(x))\). Then \(h_n\circ G_n\xrightarrow{e}h\circ G\). The sequential continuity condition on \(G_n\) transfers the epi-liminf inequality, while the displayed recovery-lifting condition ensures that recovery points for \(h_n\) can be realized through the images of \(G_n\). Without this range-accessibility requirement, epi-convergence of \(h_n\) alone does not control the compositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composition preserves epi-convergence when varying inner maps transfer convergent sequences and their ranges realize recovery sequences for the outer functions.
knowledge_statements.title: Composition Qualification Regimes

children.title: Marginal Function Limits
children.top_down_role: Epi-limit behavior of value functions formed by eliminating variables.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are metric spaces and \(F_n,F:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) are proper lower semicontinuous functions.
The family is locally uniformly level-bounded in \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_n\xrightarrow{e}m\), where \(m_n(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}F_n(x,y)\) and \(m(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric-space marginalization with compactness in the eliminated variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(m_n(x):=\inf_{y\in Y}F_n(x,y)\) and \(m(x):=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\). Suppose that for every \(x\in X\), every sequence \(x_n\to x\), and every real \(\alpha\), all sufficiently large sets \(\{y:F_n(x_n,y)\leq\alpha\}\) lie in one sequentially compact subset of \(Y\). Then \(m_n\xrightarrow{e}m\). In particular, bounded-value almost-minimizers cannot escape in the eliminated variable, so their cluster points supply the marginal epi-liminf inequality, while recovery sequences for \(F_n\) yield the marginal epi-limsup inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epi-convergence passes to marginal infima when bounded-value almost-minimizers remain compact in the eliminated variable.
knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Function Limits

children.title: Infimal Operation Limits
children.top_down_role: Epi-limit behavior under infimum-based function constructions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed space and \(f_n,g_n,f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
The family \((H_n)\) is locally uniformly level-bounded in \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n\mathbin{\square}g_n\xrightarrow{e}f\mathbin{\square}g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infimal-convolution limit obtained as a qualified marginal limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in X\), define \((f_n\mathbin{\square}g_n)(x):=\inf_{y\in X}\{f_n(y)+g_n(x-y)\}\) and define \(f\mathbin{\square}g\) analogously. If \(H_n\xrightarrow{e}H\) on \(X\times X\) and, for every convergent \(x_n\to x\) and real \(\alpha\), the sets \(\{y:H_n(x_n,y)\leq\alpha\}\) are eventually contained in one compact set, then \(f_n\mathbin{\square}g_n\xrightarrow{e}f\mathbin{\square}g\). Thus both algebraic compatibility and compactness of near-optimal decompositions are required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infimal convolutions epi-converge when the lifted sums epi-converge and bounded-value decompositions cannot escape to infinity.
knowledge_statements.title: Infimal Operation Limits

children.title: Epigraph Projection Limits
children.top_down_role: Set-limit behavior arising from projection of epigraphical representations.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are metric spaces and \(F_n,F:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) are proper lower semicontinuous functions.
For every \(x_n\to x\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), the sections \(\{y\in Y:F_n(x_n,y)\leq\alpha\}\) are eventually contained in one sequentially compact subset of \(Y\).
Every nonempty finite sublevel section of each \(F_n\) and of \(F\) in the variable \(y\) is compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(m_n(x):=\inf_{y\in Y}F_n(x,y)\) and \(m(x):=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\), one has \(\operatorname{epi}m_n=\pi_{X\times\mathbb R}(\operatorname{epi}F_n)\), \(\operatorname{epi}m=\pi_{X\times\mathbb R}(\operatorname{epi}F)\), and \(\operatorname{epi}m_n\to\operatorname{epi}m\) in the Painleve-Kuratowski sense.

notation.meaning: projection deleting the variable in Y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualified convergence of projected epigraphs representing marginal functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(m_n(x):=\inf_{y\in Y}F_n(x,y)\), \(m(x):=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\), and \(\pi_{X\times\mathbb R}(x,y,\alpha):=(x,\alpha)\). Compactness and lower semicontinuity ensure attainment of every finite marginal infimum, so \(\operatorname{epi}m_n=\pi_{X\times\mathbb R}(\operatorname{epi}F_n)\) and \(\operatorname{epi}m=\pi_{X\times\mathbb R}(\operatorname{epi}F)\). Under the stated local uniform compactness condition, \(m_n\xrightarrow{e}m\), equivalently \(\operatorname{epi}m_n\to\operatorname{epi}m\) in the Painleve-Kuratowski sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compact eliminated-variable sections make marginal epigraphs exact projections, and local uniform compactness makes those projected epigraphs converge under epi-convergence of the original functions.
knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Projection Limits

children.title: Eliminated-Variable Compactness
children.top_down_role: Compactness regimes controlling variable elimination in these operations.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are metric spaces and \(F_n:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bounded marginal values along \(x_n\to x\) force associated eliminated variables to have convergent subsequences.

notation.meaning: sublevel section in the eliminated variable

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential local uniform level-boundedness in the eliminated variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Write \(L_n(x,\alpha):=\{y\in Y:F_n(x,y)\leq\alpha\}\). The sequence is locally uniformly level-bounded in the eliminated variable if, for every \(x\in X\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(x\), a sequentially compact set \(K\subset Y\), and \(N\in\mathbb N\) such that
\[L_n(x',\alpha)\subset K\quad\text{for all }x'\in U\text{ and }n\geq N.\]
Equivalently in proper metric spaces, any \(x_n\to x\) and \(y_n\) with \(\sup_nF_n(x_n,y_n)<+\infty\) have an eliminated-variable subsequence converging in \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminated-variable compactness requires uniformly bounded sublevel sections near each retained variable, preventing bounded-value witnesses from escaping.
knowledge_statements.title: Eliminated-Variable Compactness

assumptions_latex: Functions take values in \(\overline{\mathbb R}\) on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Epi-convergence is not preserved by pointwise addition without a common-recovery qualification.

notation.meaning: indicator taking zero on the set and positive infinity outside

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of epi-continuity for addition through incompatible recovery sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f_n:=\delta_{\{0\}}\) and \(g_n:=\delta_{\{1/n\}}\) on \(\mathbb R\). Then \(f_n\xrightarrow{e}\delta_{\{0\}}\) and \(g_n\xrightarrow{e}\delta_{\{0\}}\). However, the two finite domains are disjoint for every \(n\), so
\[f_n+g_n\equiv+\infty,\]
whereas \(\delta_{\{0\}}+\delta_{\{0\}}=\delta_{\{0\}}\). Hence \(f_n+g_n\) does not epi-converge to the sum of the epi-limits. The failure is precisely the absence of a sequence that simultaneously recovers both limiting values at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two epi-convergent indicator sequences can have disjoint finite domains, making every approximating sum infinite although the sum of their limits is finite.
knowledge_statements.title: Epi-Operation Failure Regimes

children.title: Gamma-Convergence
children.top_down_role: The calculus-of-variations organization of topological variational convergence, compactness, and asymptotic minimization.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Gamma-convergence and K-convergence; comparison with pointwise convergence; convergence of minima and minimizers

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological space and \(F_n:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_n\) topologically Gamma-converges to \(F\) exactly when its neighborhood Gamma-liminf and Gamma-limsup both equal \(F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhood definition valid without assuming first countability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in X\), define
\[(\Gamma\!\operatorname{-liminf}_nF_n)(x):=\sup_{U\in\mathcal N(x)}\liminf_{n\to\infty}\inf_{y\in U}F_n(y),\]
and define \(\Gamma\!\operatorname{-limsup}_nF_n\) by replacing \(\liminf\) with \(\limsup\). The sequence topologically Gamma-converges to \(F:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), written \(F_n\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F\), when
\[\Gamma\!\operatorname{-liminf}_nF_n=F=\Gamma\!\operatorname{-limsup}_nF_n\]
pointwise on \(X\). This neighborhood formulation remains meaningful when convergent sequences do not determine the topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Topological Gamma-convergence means that the neighborhood-based Gamma-liminf and Gamma-limsup coincide pointwise with the limiting functional.
knowledge_statements.title: Topological Gamma-Convergence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The neighborhood formula is mathematically plausible, but the cited epi-convergence section does not establish support for the claimed arbitrary-topological-space Gamma formulation. A source treating topological Gamma-limits beyond sequential or metrizable settings is required.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a first-countable topological space and \(F_n,F:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_n\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F\) sequentially if and only if the liminf and recovery-sequence conditions hold at every point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential characterization on first-countable spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sequence \(F_n\) sequentially Gamma-converges to \(F\) if, for every \(x\in X\), both conditions hold: first, every sequence \(x_n\to x\) satisfies
\[F(x)\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}F_n(x_n);\]
second, there exists a recovery sequence \(x_n\to x\) satisfying
\[F(x)\geq\limsup_{n\to\infty}F_n(x_n).\]
Together these inequalities force convergence of the recovery values whenever \(F(x)\) is finite. First countability ensures equivalence with the neighborhood definition of topological Gamma-convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential Gamma-convergence consists of a liminf inequality along every convergent sequence and a matching limsup inequality along at least one recovery sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Gamma-Convergence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sequential liminf and recovery conditions are standard, but the cited source locator does not reliably support the stated equivalence with neighborhood Gamma-convergence on every first-countable topological space. A source with that exact topological scope is required.

children.title: Gamma-Type Functional Convergence
children.top_down_role: Functional convergence viewed through Gamma-type variational limits.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space and \(F_n,F:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Gamma-type convergence predicate is the conjunction of the universal liminf inequality and pointwise recovery.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Functional inequalities underlying Gamma-convergence in metric spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Gamma-type functional convergence to \(F\) requires, at every \(x\in X\),
\[F(x)\leq\inf_{x_n\to x}\liminf_{n\to\infty}F_n(x_n)\]
and
\[F(x)\geq\inf_{x_n\to x}\limsup_{n\to\infty}F_n(x_n).\]
The first inequality is equivalent to the liminf inequality along every sequence converging to \(x\); the second asserts existence of arbitrarily accurate recovery sequences and, in metric spaces, may be realized by one diagonal recovery sequence. Equality of the resulting Gamma-lower and Gamma-upper limits with \(F\) is Gamma-convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gamma-type convergence compares function values along all converging sequences for the lower bound and along a selected recovery sequence for the upper bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Gamma-Type Functional Convergence

children.title: Kuratowski-Type Functional Convergence
children.top_down_role: Functional convergence represented through Kuratowski limits of associated sets.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space and \(F_n,F:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) are lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Kuratowski-type functional convergence is Painleve–Kuratowski convergence of \(\operatorname{epi}F_n\) to \(\operatorname{epi}F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Functional convergence encoded by Kuratowski limits of epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Equip \(X\times\mathbb R\) with the product topology. Kuratowski-type functional convergence of \(F_n\) to \(F\) means
\[\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{epi}F_n\subseteq\operatorname{epi}F\subseteq\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{epi}F_n.\]
Equivalently, the outer and inner Painleve–Kuratowski limits of the epigraphs both equal \(\operatorname{epi}F\). The outer inclusion excludes limiting epigraph points below \(F\), while the inner inclusion requires every point of the limiting epigraph to be approximated by points in the epigraphs of \(F_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Kuratowski-type functional convergence means that the inner and outer set limits of the epigraphs coincide with the epigraph of the limit function.
knowledge_statements.title: Kuratowski-Type Functional Convergence

children.title: Functional–Set Limit Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The representation bridge between functional limits and associated set limits.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space and \(F_n,F:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) are lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_n\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F\) if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}F_n\to\operatorname{epi}F\) in the Painleve-Kuratowski sense.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric-space equivalence between Gamma-convergence and epigraph set convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The following are equivalent: \(F_n\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F\); and \(\operatorname{epi}F_n\to\operatorname{epi}F\) in the Painleve-Kuratowski sense in \(X\times\mathbb R\). More explicitly, the sequential Gamma-liminf condition corresponds to \(\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{epi}F_n\subseteq\operatorname{epi}F\), and the recovery condition corresponds to \(\operatorname{epi}F\subseteq\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{epi}F_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In metric spaces, Gamma-convergence of lower-semicontinuous functions is equivalent to Painleve-Kuratowski convergence of their epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.title: Functional–Set Limit Correspondence

children.title: Gamma-Compactness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Precompact families under Gamma-type convergence.

assumptions_latex: \(F_n:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is a sequence of extended-real-valued functionals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist indices \(n_k\uparrow\infty\) and \(F:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) such that \(F_{n_k}\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F\); under equicoercivity, \(F\) is coercive and almost-minimizers are relatively compact.

notation.meaning: Gamma-convergence in the metric topology of X
Every bounded-energy sequence lies eventually in a common relatively compact set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential compactness in the Gamma topology, with equicoercivity supplying compactness of bounded-energy sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(X\) is separable and metrizable, every sequence \((F_n)\) with \(F_n:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) has a subsequence \((F_{n_k})\) and a functional \(F:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) such that \(F_{n_k}\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F\). If, additionally, for every \(t\in\mathbb R\) there is a relatively compact \(K_t\subset X\) with \(\{x:F_n(x)\le t\}\subset K_t\) for all \(n\), then \(F\) has relatively compact sublevel sets. Moreover, any sequence \((x_k)\) satisfying \(F_{n_k}(x_k)-\inf_XF_{n_k}\to0\) has cluster points, and every cluster point minimizes \(F\), provided the infima are finite and uniformly bounded above.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a separable metric space, functionals admit a Gamma-convergent subsequence. Equicoercivity makes the limit coercive and gives compactness and consistency of almost-minimizers.
knowledge_statements.title: Gamma-Compactness Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits the Gamma-compactness-regimes leaf and is mathematically plausible, but the broad subsequence compactness theorem and the equicoercive almost-minimizer conclusions require an inspectable authoritative citation with a specific theorem or section locator.

children.title: Subsequence Gamma-Limits
children.top_down_role: Variational limits obtained along selected subsequences.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The subsequence has Gamma-limit \(F\) exactly when its sequential Gamma-liminf and Gamma-limsup both equal \(F\) at every \(x\in X\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: sequential Gamma-liminf and Gamma-limsup definition
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential metric-space definition along a fixed increasing index subsequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(x\in X\), define
\[(\Gamma\!\operatorname{-liminf}_{k}F_{n_k})(x)=\inf_{x_k\to x}\liminf_{k\to\infty}F_{n_k}(x_k),\qquad (\Gamma\!\operatorname{-limsup}_{k}F_{n_k})(x)=\inf_{x_k\to x}\limsup_{k\to\infty}F_{n_k}(x_k).\]
The subsequence \((F_{n_k})\) Gamma-converges to \(F:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) when, for every \(x\in X\), both displayed quantities equal \(F(x)\). Equivalently, every sequence \(x_k\to x\) satisfies \(F(x)\le\liminf_kF_{n_k}(x_k)\), and at least one recovery sequence \(x_k\to x\) satisfies \(F(x)\ge\limsup_kF_{n_k}(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subsequence Gamma-converges when its variational lower and upper limits coincide pointwise, equivalently when the lower-bound and recovery-sequence conditions both hold.
knowledge_statements.title: Subsequence Gamma-Limits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition, quantifiers, and sequential Gamma-liminf/Gamma-limsup formulas are consistent with the metric-space setting and fit the leaf. No source reference with a specific locator is attached, so the stated equivalence cannot yet pass citation review.

children.title: Limit Identification Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural settings used to distinguish or identify subsequential Gamma-limits.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If every subsequence of \((F_n)\) contains a further subsequence Gamma-converging to \(F\), then \(F_n\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F\).

notation.meaning: An arbitrary increasing subsequence of indices

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: subsequence characterization of convergence in the sequential Gamma topology
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subsequence criterion for identifying a unique Gamma-limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose that for every increasing sequence \((n_k)\) there is a further subsequence \((n_{k_j})\) such that \(F_{n_{k_j}}\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F\), with the same functional \(F\) independent of the chosen subsequence. Then the full sequence satisfies \(F_n\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F\). Consequently, after Gamma-compactness has supplied subsequential limits, it suffices to identify every such limit with one candidate \(F\). Identification may be established by matching the Gamma-liminf lower bound and constructing recovery sequences for that candidate on every extracted subsequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The full sequence Gamma-converges to a candidate if every subsequence has a further subsequence with that same Gamma-limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Limit Identification Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The subsequence identification principle fits the terminal container and is correctly formulated with a common limit independent of the extracted subsequence. An inspectable source for the Gamma-convergence subsequence criterion is still required.

children.title: Integral-Representation Interfaces for Gamma-Limits
children.top_down_role: Detailed localization and integral-representation theory belongs to the integral-functionals chapter.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) has the displayed local integral representation on \(W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At Lebesgue points, the integrand is recovered by \(f(x,\xi)=\lim_{\rho\downarrow0}F(\ell_{x,\xi},Q_\rho(x))/|Q_\rho(x)|\).

notation.meaning: Cube centered at x with side length ρ

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface only: localization identifies an already-established integral Gamma-limit; existence hypotheses are deferred.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume a localized Gamma-limit \(F\) satisfies
\[F(u,A)=\int_A f(x,\nabla u(x))\,dx\]
for every open \(A\subset\Omega\) and \(u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\), where \(f\) has suitable measurable dependence on \(x\) and continuous dependence on the gradient variable. For \(\xi\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\), set \(\ell_{x,\xi}(y)=\xi(y-x)\). At every Lebesgue point \(x\) of \(y\mapsto f(y,\xi)\), the density is identified by
\[f(x,\xi)=\lim_{\rho\downarrow0}\frac{F(\ell_{x,\xi},Q_\rho(x))}{|Q_\rho(x)|}.\]
The separate integral-representation theorem must establish locality, measure structure, growth, and lower semicontinuity sufficient for the assumed representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once a Gamma-limit is known to be a local integral functional, its density is identified by normalized energies of affine maps on shrinking cubes.
knowledge_statements.title: Integral-Representation Interfaces for Gamma-Limits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record appropriately presents a localization interface rather than an integral-representation existence theorem, and the shrinking-cube formula follows from the assumed representation at Lebesgue points. A source is needed to verify the precise admissibility and localization hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Mosco lower bounds use \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\), while recovery conditions require \(x_n\to x\) in norm.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: defining strong-recovery and weak-liminf geometry of Mosco convergence
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reflexive Banach-space geometry underlying Mosco convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Mosco convergence combines two different topologies on \(X\). Its closedness or lower-bound clause is tested against arbitrary weakly convergent sequences \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\), whereas its attainability or recovery clause requires a sequence converging strongly, \(x_n\to x\). Since strong convergence implies weak convergence, the recovery requirement is more restrictive topologically, while the weak lower-bound requirement tests more sequences. Reflexivity ensures that norm-bounded sequences have weakly convergent subsequences, which makes this strong–weak pairing effective in compactness arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mosco convergence tests lower bounds along weakly convergent sequences but demands norm-convergent recovery sequences; reflexivity supplies weak subsequential compactness for bounded sequences.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong–Weak Topological Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strong-recovery/weak-liminf geometry is accurately stated and the principle content kind fits this conceptual leaf. The reflexive compactness assertion and Mosco convention need a cited textbook section or other inspectable source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak-topological notions in Hilbert spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collects weak openness, convergence, closedness, compactness, continuity, and lower semicontinuity, including the infinite-dimensional unboundedness boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a Hilbert space. A set is weakly open iff it is a union of finite intersections of open half-spaces. If \(\dim\mathcal H=\infty\), every nonempty finite intersection of open half-spaces, and hence every nonempty weakly open set, is unbounded. A net \((x_a)\) converges weakly to \(x\), written \(x_a\rightharpoonup x\), iff \(\langle x_a,u\rangle\to\langle x,u\rangle\) for every \(u\in\mathcal H\). A set \(C\subseteq\mathcal H\) is weakly closed iff every weak limit of a net in \(C\) lies in \(C\), and weakly compact iff every net in \(C\) has a weak cluster point in \(C\). It is weakly sequentially closed iff every weak limit of a sequence in \(C\) lies in \(C\), and weakly sequentially compact iff every sequence in \(C\) has a weak sequential cluster point in \(C\). If \(D\subseteq\mathcal H\) is nonempty, \(\mathcal K\) is a real Hilbert space, and \(T:D\to\mathcal K\), then \(T\) is weakly continuous iff \(x_a\rightharpoonup x\in D\) implies \(Tx_a\rightharpoonup Tx\) for every net in \(D\). For \(f:\mathcal H\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), weak lower semicontinuity at \(x\) means that every net \(x_a\rightharpoonup x\) satisfies \(f(x)\leq\liminf_a f(x_a)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weakly open sets are unions of finite intersections of open half-spaces; in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space every nonempty weakly open set is unbounded. Weak convergence is pointwise convergence of all inner products. Weak closedness, compactness, their sequential counterparts, weak continuity, and weak lower semicontinuity are characterized by the stated net or sequence conditions.
assumptions_latex: For weak continuity, \(D\subseteq\mathcal H\) is nonempty, \(\mathcal K\) is a real Hilbert space, and \(T:D\to\mathcal K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_a\rightharpoonup x\iff(\forall u\in\mathcal H)\;\langle x_a,u\rangle\to\langle x,u\rangle,\quad f(x)\leq\liminf_a f(x_a)\text{ for weak lower semicontinuity, with the stated net and sequence characterizations of the other weak-topological notions.}
