assumptions_latex: \(C_n,C\subset X\) are nonempty closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_n\xrightarrow{M}C\) exactly when strong recovery and weak outer closedness both hold.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical Mosco convergence definition for closed convex sets
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical sequential definition for nonempty closed convex subsets of a reflexive Banach space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence \((C_n)\) Mosco-converges to \(C\), written \(C_n\xrightarrow{M}C\), if both conditions hold. First, for every \(x\in C\), there exist \(x_n\in C_n\) such that \(x_n\to x\) in norm. Second, whenever \((n_k)\) is increasing, \(x_k\in C_{n_k}\), and \(x_k\rightharpoonup x\) weakly in \(X\), one has \(x\in C\). Thus every limit point is strongly approximable from the moving sets, while no weak subsequential limit of their points lies outside \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed convex sets Mosco-converge when every limit point has strong approximants and every weak limit of points selected from the moving sets belongs to the limit set.
knowledge_statements.title: Mosco Convergence of Convex Sets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is the standard sequential definition of Mosco convergence for closed convex sets in a reflexive Banach space, with explicit strong inner and weak outer conditions. It lacks an attached authoritative citation with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n\xrightarrow{M}f\) exactly when the weak liminf inequality and strong recovery condition hold at every \(x\in X\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical Mosco convergence definition for convex functions
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on a reflexive Banach space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The functions \((f_n)\) Mosco-converge to \(f\), written \(f_n\xrightarrow{M}f\), if for every \(x\in X\) the following two conditions hold. For every sequence \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\),
\[f(x)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n(x_n).\]
There also exists a sequence \(y_n\to x\) in norm such that
\[f(x)\ge\limsup_{n\to\infty}f_n(y_n).\]
Together the inequalities imply \(f_n(y_n)\to f(x)\) whenever \(f(x)\) is finite. The first clause is the weak lower bound and the second is the strong recovery condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex functions Mosco-converge when weakly convergent sequences satisfy the lower bound and every point admits a norm-convergent recovery sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Mosco Convergence of Convex Functions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weak liminf and strong recovery clauses are correctly quantified, and the observation about convergence along a finite-valued recovery sequence follows from the two inequalities. A specific authoritative source locator is absent.

children.title: Mosco Convergence of Graphs
children.top_down_role: Mosco limits for graph representations of relations or mappings.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The graphs Mosco-converge exactly when graph points have strong recovery and weak graph limits remain in the limiting graph.

notation.meaning: Mosco convergence in the product Hilbert space

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Mosco set convergence applied in the product Hilbert space
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graphs are treated as subsets of the product Hilbert space with componentwise strong and weak topologies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The graphs of \((A_n)\) Mosco-converge to the graph of \(A\) when \(\operatorname{gra}A_n\xrightarrow{M}\operatorname{gra}A\) as subsets of \(H\times H\). Explicitly, every \((x,u)\in\operatorname{gra}A\) admits \((x_n,u_n)\in\operatorname{gra}A_n\) with \((x_n,u_n)\to(x,u)\) strongly in \(H\times H\). Conversely, if \((x_k,u_k)\in\operatorname{gra}A_{n_k}\) and \((x_k,u_k)\rightharpoonup(x,u)\) weakly in \(H\times H\), then \((x,u)\in\operatorname{gra}A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Operator graphs Mosco-converge as subsets of the product space: graph points have strong approximants, and weak graph limits remain in the limiting graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Mosco Convergence of Graphs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition consistently applies sequential set Mosco convergence in the product Hilbert space and fits the graph leaf. Because conventions for graph convergence vary, an exact source for this product-space Mosco convention is required.

children.title: Mosco Convergence of Sets
children.top_down_role: Mosco limits for set families beyond the dedicated convex-set treatment.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_n\xrightarrow{M}S\) precisely when the strong inner limit contains \(S\) and the weak outer limit is contained in \(S\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: sequential Mosco convergence for subsets of a reflexive Banach space
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-level Mosco convergence without imposing convexity; limits are interpreted sequentially.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[\operatorname{s\!\!-Li}S_n=\{x:\exists x_n\in S_n,\ x_n\to x\},\]
and let \(\operatorname{w\!\!-Ls}S_n\) consist of all \(x\in X\) for which some increasing \((n_k)\) and points \(x_k\in S_{n_k}\) satisfy \(x_k\rightharpoonup x\). The sets \((S_n)\) Mosco-converge to \(S\), written \(S_n\xrightarrow{M}S\), when
\[S\subset\operatorname{s\!\!-Li}S_n\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{w\!\!-Ls}S_n\subset S.\]
The first inclusion is strong attainability; the second excludes extraneous weak subsequential limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set Mosco convergence means every limit-set point is strongly attainable and every weak subsequential limit selected from the moving sets belongs to the limit set.
knowledge_statements.title: Mosco Convergence of Sets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strong sequential inner limit and weak sequential outer limit are explicitly defined, and their inclusions correctly express set Mosco convergence in the stated convention. The record still lacks an inspectable citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Mosco Convergence of Operators
children.top_down_role: Mosco-type convergence interfaces for operator families.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_n\xrightarrow{M}A\) means \(\operatorname{gra}A_n\xrightarrow{M}\operatorname{gra}A\) in \(H\times H\).

notation.meaning: Mosco convergence of operators through their graphs

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-based convention for Mosco convergence of set-valued operators on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the graph-based convention, a sequence of set-valued operators \((A_n)\) Mosco-converges to \(A\), written \(A_n\xrightarrow{M}A\), precisely when
\[\operatorname{gra}A_n\xrightarrow{M}\operatorname{gra}A\]
as subsets of the product Hilbert space \(H\times H\). Thus every pair \((x,u)\) satisfying \(u\in A(x)\) is the strong limit of pairs \((x_n,u_n)\) with \(u_n\in A_n(x_n)\), and every weak subsequential limit of such graph pairs satisfies \(u\in A(x)\). This convention must be distinguished from weaker strong graph convergence or resolvent convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the graph-based convention, operators Mosco-converge exactly when their graphs Mosco-converge in the product Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.title: Mosco Convergence of Operators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The graph-based definition is internally precise and fits the operator leaf, but operator Mosco terminology is not uniform across sources. A citation establishing this exact convention and distinguishing it from graph or resolvent convergence is required.

children.title: Graph–Operator Transfer
children.top_down_role: Transfer of Mosco-limit information between operators and their graphs.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\lambda>0\) and \(z\in H\), \((I+\lambda A_n)^{-1}z\to(I+\lambda A)^{-1}z\) strongly in \(H\).

notation.meaning: Resolvent of A at parameter λ

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Theorem transferring graph-level Mosco convergence to pointwise strong resolvent convergence for maximal monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_n\) and \(A\) be maximal monotone operators on \(H\), and suppose \(\operatorname{gra}A_n\xrightarrow{M}\operatorname{gra}A\) in \(H\times H\). For every \(\lambda>0\), maximal monotonicity makes the resolvents \(J_{\lambda A_n}=(I+\lambda A_n)^{-1}\) and \(J_{\lambda A}=(I+\lambda A)^{-1}\) single-valued on \(H\). Then, for each \(z\in H\), \[J_{\lambda A_n}z\to J_{\lambda A}z\quad\text{strongly in }H.\] Hence graph-level Mosco convergence transfers to pointwise strong convergence of the associated resolvent operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For maximal monotone operators, Mosco convergence of graphs yields pointwise strong convergence of every positive-parameter resolvent.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph–Operator Transfer

children.title: Dual-Space Mosco Convergence
children.top_down_role: Mosco convergence formulated on dual spaces or dual objects.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_n\xrightarrow{M}g\) on \(X^*\) exactly when weak dual-space lower bounds and norm-strong recovery sequences hold.

notation.meaning: Weak convergence in the reflexive dual space

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Mosco function convergence applied to the reflexive dual space
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mosco convergence on the dual of a reflexive Banach space, using weak and dual-norm topologies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The functions \((g_n)\) Mosco-converge to \(g:X^*\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) if, for every \(x^*\in X^*\), both dual-space conditions hold. Whenever \(x_n^*\rightharpoonup x^*\) weakly in \(X^*\),
\[g(x^*)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}g_n(x_n^*).\]
There also exists \(y_n^*\in X^*\) with \(\|y_n^*-x^*\|_{X^*}\to0\) and
\[g(x^*)\ge\limsup_{n\to\infty}g_n(y_n^*).\]
Because \(X\) is reflexive, the weak topology on \(X^*\) agrees with its weak-star topology induced by \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a reflexive dual space, Mosco convergence combines weak dual-space lower bounds with recovery sequences converging in the dual norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Space Mosco Convergence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly applies Mosco convergence to the reflexive dual space, and reflexivity justifies identifying its weak and weak-star topologies through the canonical embedding. A specific authoritative source locator is absent.

children.title: Conjugate Mosco Convergence
children.top_down_role: Mosco convergence of convex conjugate function families.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n^*\xrightarrow{M}f^*\) on \(H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space Fenchel conjugacy; no nonconvex or nonreflexive extension is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every sequence \(y_n\rightharpoonup y\), one has \(f^*(y)\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n^*(y_n)\). For every \(y\in H\), there exists \(y_n\to y\) such that \(f^*(y)\geq\limsup_{n\to\infty}f_n^*(y_n)\). Thus Fenchel conjugation preserves Mosco convergence within the class of proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For proper closed convex functions on a Hilbert space, Mosco convergence of the primal functions implies Mosco convergence of their Fenchel conjugates.
knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate Mosco Convergence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Hilbert-space Mosco-conjugacy theorem is mathematically standard and the theorem content kind fits the leaf, but the record has no citation. An authoritative theorem or section locator for preservation of Mosco convergence under Fenchel conjugation is required.

children.title: Primal–Dual Mosco Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Transfer of Mosco convergence between primal and dual representations.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space identified with its continuous dual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n\xrightarrow{M}f\iff f_n^*\xrightarrow{M}f^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attouch-type primal–dual equivalence in a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The primal and conjugate sequences satisfy the equivalence \[f_n\xrightarrow{M}f\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f_n^*\xrightarrow{M}f^*.\] In either direction, the liminf inequality is tested along weakly convergent sequences and the recovery condition uses strongly convergent sequences. The reverse implication follows at the statement level from the same preservation law applied to the conjugates together with \(f_n^{**}=f_n\) and \(f^{**}=f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mosco convergence of proper closed convex functions is equivalent to Mosco convergence of their Fenchel conjugates.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Mosco Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The duality content kind and primal-dual equivalence fit the leaf, but no source is supplied for the Attouch-type equivalence. The final sentence also gives proof-level justification and should be removed when a sourced record is submitted.

children.title: Relationships Among Variational Convergence Modes
children.top_down_role: Correspondences, specializations, and nonequivalence boundaries among epigraphical, Gamma, Mosco, and graphical limits.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{epi}}f\iff f_n\xrightarrow{\Gamma}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential correspondence on metric spaces with the same topology for both modes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The following are equivalent: \(f_n\) epi-converges to \(f\), and \(f_n\) Gamma-converges to \(f\). Explicitly, for every \(x_n\to x\), \(f(x)\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n(x_n)\), while for every \(x\in X\) there exists a recovery sequence \(x_n\to x\) satisfying \(f(x)\geq\limsup_{n\to\infty}f_n(x_n)\). Thus the two names encode the same sequential variational convergence predicate under these conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a metric space, sequential epi-convergence and Gamma convergence coincide when both use the same topology.
knowledge_statements.title: Epi–Gamma Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is correct under the stated convention that Gamma convergence is the sequential liminf/recovery-sequence notion for the same metric topology. However, the cited Rockafellar-Wets locator does not inspectably support the asserted arbitrary-metric-space scope; a source explicitly treating metric spaces or a restriction to the source-supported domain is required.

assumptions_latex: Mosco convergence uses weak liminf tests and strong recovery sequences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n\xrightarrow{M}f\Rightarrow f_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{epi}}f\), with equivalence when \(\dim H<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison with epi-convergence in the Hilbert-space strong topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f_n\xrightarrow{M}f\), then \(f_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{epi}}f\) for the norm topology, because every strongly convergent sequence is weakly convergent and the Mosco recovery sequence is strong. If \(H\) is finite-dimensional, weak and strong sequential convergence coincide, so the two convergence modes are equivalent. In infinite dimension the converse can fail because strong epi-convergence does not test weakly convergent, non-strong sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mosco convergence implies norm epi-convergence; the two coincide in finite dimension but can differ in infinite dimension.
knowledge_statements.title: Epi–Mosco Comparison

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The comparison is mathematically correct for the stated sequential definitions, and property is an appropriate kind. The supplied epi-convergence locator does not inspectably support the infinite-dimensional Hilbert-space Mosco comparison, and the statement contains explanatory proof text. A specific Mosco comparison source is required before textual revision.

assumptions_latex: Epigraphs are viewed as closed subsets of \(X\times\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{epi}}f\iff \operatorname{epi}f_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{PK}}\operatorname{epi}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraphical representation through Painlevé–Kuratowski convergence of closed sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Epi-convergence of \(f_n\) to \(f\) is equivalent to Painlevé–Kuratowski convergence \[\operatorname{epi}f_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{PK}}\operatorname{epi}f\] in the product space \(X\times\mathbb R\). Consequently, epi-convergence is a set-convergence construction applied to epigraphs. This differs from graphical convergence of a mapping, which instead applies set convergence to its graph, although both are instances of the same closed-set limiting mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epi-convergence is exactly Painlevé–Kuratowski convergence of epigraphs, paralleling graphical convergence of graphs.
knowledge_statements.title: Epi-Convergence as a Graphical-Limit Neighbor

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is the correct kind, but the arbitrary-metric-space equivalence with Painleve-Kuratowski convergence of epigraphs is broader than the inspectable scope established by the cited inventory entries. A source explicitly supporting this domain and product-space formulation is required.

children.title: Mode-Separation Examples
children.top_down_role: Examples distinguishing pairs of variational convergence modes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{epi}}f\) but \(f_n\not\xrightarrow{M}f\).

notation.meaning: Canonical unit vector in sequence space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete separation of norm epi-convergence from Mosco convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every strongly convergent sequence \(x_n\to x\), one has \(\langle x_n,e_n\rangle\to0\), so \(f_n(x_n)\to f(x)\); hence \(f_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{epi}}f\). However, \(e_n\rightharpoonup0\) and \(f_n(e_n)=-1\), giving \[f(0)=0>\liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n(e_n)=-1.\] The weak liminf condition required for Mosco convergence therefore fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear functionals along an orthonormal basis epi-converge strongly to zero but fail the weak liminf condition for Mosco convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Mode-Separation Examples

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is mathematically coherent and counterexample is the exact role for this leaf. The cited general epi-convergence section does not inspectably contain this example, while the statement is largely a proof of it. Supply a locator for this example or an authoritative source supporting the construction, then restate only the counterexample and its separation conclusion.

children.title: Nonequivalence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural settings where convergence modes fail to coincide.

assumptions_latex: Epi-convergence uses the norm topology; Mosco convergence uses weak liminf and strong recovery.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite-dimensional equivalence need not extend to infinite-dimensional \(H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension marks the basic equivalence boundary for strong epi and Mosco convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When \(\dim H<\infty\), weak and norm convergence agree sequentially, and norm epi-convergence is equivalent to Mosco convergence. When \(H\) is infinite-dimensional, norm epi-convergence alone need not imply Mosco convergence. The separating mechanism is the existence of bounded sequences \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\) that do not converge to \(x\) in norm, leaving their values uncontrolled by the strong epi-liminf condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong epi and Mosco convergence coincide in finite dimension but are generally nonequivalent in infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonequivalence Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary is an appropriate kind and the finite/infinite-dimensional distinction is correct. The cited locator does not inspectably support the infinite-dimensional nonequivalence regime, so a specific source for that boundary or its counterexample is required.

children.title: One-Way Implication Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings supporting only a directional implication between modes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n\xrightarrow{M}f\Rightarrow f_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{epi}}f\), whereas the converse requires additional hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal implication and its nonreversible infinite-dimensional boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Mosco convergence always implies norm epi-convergence: its weak liminf inequality applies in particular to every norm-convergent sequence, and its recovery sequence already converges in norm. The reverse implication is not valid on arbitrary infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, because norm epi-convergence supplies no liminf control along sequences that converge only weakly. It becomes valid whenever the relevant weak and strong sequential tests coincide, notably in finite dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mosco convergence always implies norm epi-convergence, but the reverse generally fails unless weak and strong tests coincide.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Way Implication Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The one-way implication is correct, although property would be a more exact mathematical role than principle. The cited locator does not inspectably support the Hilbert-space Mosco implication and the statement includes proof-level explanation; a specific source is needed before replacement.

children.title: Topology-Driven Separation
children.top_down_role: Separation caused by changes in ambient or mixed topologies.

assumptions_latex: \(H=\ell^2\) is equipped with its norm and weak topologies.
\((e_n)\) denotes the canonical orthonormal basis of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_n\rightharpoonup 0\) while \(e_n\not\to 0\) in norm, so weak-liminf and strong-liminf tests can distinguish convergence modes.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The separation mechanism is the distinction between weak and norm sequential convergence in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(H=\ell^2\), the canonical basis satisfies \(e_n\rightharpoonup 0\) and \(\lVert e_n\rVert=1\) for every \(n\). Thus weakly convergent sequences that are not norm convergent provide the topological mechanism by which a weak-liminf condition can be strictly stronger than the corresponding norm-liminf condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weakly convergent sequences that do not converge in norm create the topological distinction underlying separation between strong epi-convergence and Mosco convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Topology-Driven Separation

children.title: Equicoercivity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Uniform coercivity structures supporting variational compactness.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(a\in\mathbb R\), the set \(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}\{x\in X:f_n(x)\leq a\}\) is relatively compact.

notation.meaning: Sublevel set of the nth function at height a

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric-space equicoercivity expressed as uniform relative compactness of fixed-height sublevels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sequence \((f_n)\) is equicoercive if, for every \(a\in\mathbb R\), the union \(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}S_n(a)\) is relatively compact in \(X\). Equivalently, for each \(a\in\mathbb R\), there is a compact set \(K_a\subset X\) such that \(S_n(a)\subset K_a\) for every \(n\in\mathbb N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence is equicoercive when the union of all its sublevel sets at each fixed height is relatively compact, equivalently contained in one compact set.
knowledge_statements.title: Equicoercivity Regimes

children.title: Minimizing-Sequence Compactness
children.top_down_role: Precompactness behavior of exact or approximate minimizing sequences.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space and \(f_n:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) for every \(n\in\mathbb N\).
For \(m_n=\inf_{x\in X}f_n(x)\), one has \(m_n\in\mathbb R\) for every \(n\) and \(\sup_n m_n<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sequence \((x_n)\) is relatively compact in \(X\).

notation.meaning: Optimal value of the nth problem

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compactness of vanishing-error approximate minimizers under equicoercivity and a uniform upper bound on optimal values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \((f_n)\) is equicoercive, \(\sup_n m_n<+\infty\), and \(f_n(x_n)\leq m_n+\varepsilon_n\) with \(\varepsilon_n\to0\), then the approximate-minimizer sequence \((x_n)\) is relatively compact in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equicoercivity and a uniform upper bound on the optimal values make every vanishing-error approximate-minimizer sequence relatively compact.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimizing-Sequence Compactness

children.title: Sublevel Compactness Transfer
children.top_down_role: Transfer from uniform sublevel control to compactness of minimizing sequences.

assumptions_latex: \(f_n,f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(f_n\xrightarrow{\Gamma}f\) with respect to the metric topology.
For every \(b\in\mathbb R\), there exists a compact set \(K_b\subset X\) such that \(\{x\in X:f_n(x)\leq b\}\subset K_b\) for every \(n\in\mathbb N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(a\in\mathbb R\), the sublevel set \(\{x\in X:f(x)\leq a\}\) is compact.

notation.meaning: Limit sublevel set at height a

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer of compact sublevels from a uniformly equicoercive sequence to its metric Gamma limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f_n\xrightarrow{\Gamma}f\) on the metric space \(X\) and the sequence \((f_n)\) is equicoercive in the stated common-compact-sublevel sense, then \(S(a)=\{x\in X:f(x)\leq a\}\) is compact for every \(a\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under metric Gamma convergence, uniform equicoercivity of the approximating functions transfers compact sublevels to the limit function.
knowledge_statements.title: Sublevel Compactness Transfer

assumptions_latex: The sequence \((f_n)\) is equicoercive: for every \(a\in\mathbb R\), the union \(\bigcup_n\{x:f_n(x)\le a\}\) is relatively compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_X f_n\to\inf_X f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional optimal-value stability under epigraphical convergence and equicoercivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m_n:=\inf_{x\in X}f_n(x)\) and \(m:=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\). Epigraphical convergence gives \(m\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}m_n\). For any \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), a recovery sequence \(x_n\to x\) gives \(\limsup_{n\to\infty}m_n\le f(x)\), hence \(\limsup_{n\to\infty}m_n\le m\). Equicoercivity prevents minimizing sequences from escaping and ensures that the lower bound is realized through cluster points. Consequently, \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\inf_{x\in X}f_n(x)=\inf_{x\in X}f(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For equicoercive lower-semicontinuous functions, epigraphical convergence implies convergence of their infimal values.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Value Stability

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every cluster point \(\bar x\) of \((x_n)\) lies in \(\operatorname{argmin}f\), and \(\min f_n\to\min f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer stability of exact global minimizers in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(m_n:=\min_X f_n\) and \(m:=\min_X f\). Equicoercivity makes \((x_n)\) relatively compact, and optimal-value stability gives \(m_n\to m\). If a subsequence satisfies \(x_{n_k}\to\bar x\), the epigraphical lower inequality yields \[f(\bar x)\le\liminf_{k\to\infty}f_{n_k}(x_{n_k})=\lim_{k\to\infty}m_{n_k}=m.\] Since \(m\le f(\bar x)\), equality holds and \(\bar x\in\operatorname{argmin}f\). Thus \(\limsup_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{argmin}f_n\subseteq\operatorname{argmin}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under epigraphical convergence and equicoercivity, exact minimizers are precompact and every cluster point minimizes the limit function.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Minimizer Stability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role and outer-stability claim fit Exact-Minimizer Stability, but the statement includes a proof and the citation does not identify a theorem or subsection supporting exact-minimizer stability under epi-convergence and equicoercivity. A claim-specific source is required.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every cluster point of \((x_n)\) belongs to \(\operatorname{argmin}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vanishing-error global minimizers under epigraphical convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m_n:=\inf_X f_n\) and \(m:=\inf_X f\). Equicoercivity and the approximate optimality inequality make \((x_n)\) relatively compact, while optimal-value stability gives \(m_n\to m\). For every subsequence with \(x_{n_k}\to\bar x\), \[f(\bar x)\le\liminf_{k\to\infty}f_{n_k}(x_{n_k})\le\limsup_{k\to\infty}(m_{n_k}+\varepsilon_{n_k})=m.\] Therefore \(f(\bar x)=m\), so \(\bar x\in\operatorname{argmin}f\). Equivalently, every convergent selection from the vanishing-tolerance solution sets has a limiting exact solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vanishing-tolerance minimizers are precompact under equicoercivity, and all their cluster points minimize the epigraphical limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximate-Minimizer Stability

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space, \(S:=\operatorname{argmin}f\ne\varnothing\), and \(m:=\min_X f\).
For some \(\alpha>0\) and \(p>0\), \(f(x)\ge m+\alpha d(x,S)^p\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)\le m+\varepsilon\) implies \(d(x,S)\le(\varepsilon/\alpha)^{1/p}\).

notation.meaning: distance from a point to the solution set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Growth-based distance estimate for approximate global solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the \(\varepsilon\)-solution set by \(S_\varepsilon:=\{x\in X:f(x)\le m+\varepsilon\}\) for \(\varepsilon\ge0\). The growth condition implies, for every \(x\in S_\varepsilon\), \[\alpha d(x,S)^p\le f(x)-m\le\varepsilon.\] Hence \[\sup_{x\in S_\varepsilon}d(x,S)\le\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{\alpha}\right)^{1/p}.\] Thus a functional objective-gap certificate yields a quantitative one-sided excess estimate from the approximate solution set to the exact solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A power-growth condition converts an objective gap into an explicit distance bound from approximate solutions to the exact solution set.

children.title: Escaping Minimizer Regimes
children.top_down_role: Loss of compactness through minimizing sequences leaving controlled regions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{argmin}f_n=\{n\}\) escapes every bounded set although \(\inf f_n=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete loss of minimizer compactness on a noncompact domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(n\), the function \(f_n\) is continuous and coercive, with \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}f_n(x)=0,\qquad \operatorname{argmin}f_n=\{n\}.\] The unique minimizer sequence \(x_n=n\) has no convergent subsequence and eventually leaves every bounded subset of \(\mathbb R\). Moreover, for every fixed \(x\in\mathbb R\), \(f_n(x)\to+\infty\). This family shows that individual coercivity and stable optimal values do not supply uniform minimizer compactness; an equicoercivity or common level-boundedness hypothesis is essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Individually coercive objectives can have constant optimal values while their unique minimizers escape to infinity.
knowledge_statements.title: Escaping Minimizer Regimes

children.title: Nonattainment Regimes
children.top_down_role: Limit problems or approximating problems lacking attained minima.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}f(x)=0\) but \(\operatorname{argmin}f=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonattainment caused by loss of compactness on an open direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The continuous function \(f(x)=e^x\) satisfies \(f(x)>0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R\), while \(f(-n)=e^{-n}\to0\). Consequently, \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}f(x)=0\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{argmin}f=\varnothing.\] Taking the constant sequence \(f_n=f\) gives exact epigraphical convergence and constant optimal values, yet neither the approximating nor limiting problem has a minimizer. Thus value stability alone does not imply attainment; lower semicontinuity must be paired with an appropriate compactness or level-boundedness condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even a continuous objective may have a finite infimum that is never attained, so stable values need not produce solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonattainment Regimes

children.title: Spurious-Minimizer Regimes
children.top_down_role: Limit points or approximate solutions that do not represent stable minimizers.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n(x)\to x^2\) pointwise, but \(c_n\in\operatorname{argmin}f_n\) and \(c_n\to1\notin\operatorname{argmin}(x\mapsto x^2)\).

notation.meaning: location of the moving artificial well

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise convergence permits moving wells and spurious limiting minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each fixed \(x\in\mathbb R\), equality \(x=c_n\) occurs for at most one \(n\), so \(f_n(x)\to f(x):=x^2\). Nevertheless, \[\operatorname{argmin}f_n=\{c_n\},\qquad c_n\to1,\qquad \operatorname{argmin}f=\{0\}.\] Hence the approximating minimizers converge to a point that does not minimize the pointwise limit. The downward moving wells violate the epigraphical lower-limit condition along \(c_n\to1\), since \(\liminf_n f_n(c_n)=-1<f(1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise convergence can hide moving downward wells whose minimizers converge to a nonminimizer of the limit objective.

children.title: Value–Solution Decoupling
children.top_down_role: Regimes where optimal values stabilize without corresponding minimizer stability.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scalar values \(\inf f_n=0\) converge, while the solution sets \(\operatorname{argmin}f_n=\{n\}\) have no finite outer limit point.

notation.meaning: minimizer set of the nth objective

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal-value convergence does not control the location or convergence of solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Each problem has the same optimal value but a different singleton solution set: \[m_n:=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}f_n(x)=0,\qquad S_n:=\operatorname{argmin}f_n=\{n\}.\] Thus \((m_n)\) converges, whereas no sequence \(x_n\in S_n\) has a finite cluster point and \(\limsup_n S_n=\varnothing\) in \(\mathbb R\). This separates scalar value stability from set-valued solution stability: convergence of infima alone contains no positional information about minimizers and cannot replace equicoercivity or another compactness hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convergent optimal values alone provide no control over minimizer locations or convergence of solution sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Value–Solution Decoupling

children.title: Generalized Differentiability Under Epigraphical Limits
children.top_down_role: Convergence interfaces between function limits and first- or second-order generalized variational objects.

children.title: Subderivative Limits
children.top_down_role: Variational-limit behavior of first-order subderivative objects.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and \(f(\bar x)\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(df(\bar x)(w)=\liminf_{t\downarrow0,\,w'\to w}\frac{f(\bar x+t w')-f(\bar x)}{t}\).

notation.meaning: lower subderivative of f at the base point in direction w

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower subderivative defined by joint directional difference-quotient limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(t>0\), define the first-order difference quotient by \[\Delta_t f(\bar x)(w):=\frac{f(\bar x+t w)-f(\bar x)}{t}.\] The lower subderivative of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) in direction \(w\) is the extended-real number \[df(\bar x)(w):=\liminf_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\w'\to w}}\Delta_t f(\bar x)(w').\] Equivalently, the limit inferior ranges over all sequences \(t_k\downarrow0\) and \(w_k\to w\). The perturbation \(w'\to w\) makes the definition stable under nearby directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower subderivative is the joint lower limit of first-order difference quotients as step sizes vanish and directions approach the target direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Subderivative Limits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula is a plausible finite-dimensional definition of the lower subderivative and definition is an acceptable role for this leaf. Because conventions for subderivatives and directional epi-limits vary, an authoritative definition number, section, or page is required to validate the exact joint-liminf formula and notation.

children.title: Difference-Quotient Limits
children.top_down_role: Set or function limits of first-order difference-quotient families.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and finite at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The epigraphical lower limit of \(\Delta_t f(\bar x)\) has value \(df(\bar x)(w)\) at every direction \(w\).

notation.meaning: epigraphical lower limit as t decreases to zero

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraphical lower limit of first-order difference-quotient functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(t>0\), regard \(\Delta_t f(\bar x):\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) as a function of the direction, with \[\Delta_t f(\bar x)(w):=\frac{f(\bar x+t w)-f(\bar x)}{t}.\] Its epigraphical lower limit satisfies \[\left(\operatorname{e\!\!-\!liminf}_{t\downarrow0}\Delta_t f(\bar x)\right)(w)=\liminf_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\w'\to w}}\Delta_t f(\bar x)(w')=df(\bar x)(w).\] Thus the lower subderivative is exactly the pointwise value of the epigraphical lower limit of the quotient family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Viewing each difference quotient as a function of direction, its epigraphical lower limit is the lower subderivative.
knowledge_statements.title: Difference-Quotient Limits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed identity matches the usual pointwise formula for an epigraphical lower limit, and representation fits Difference-Quotient Limits. The exact notation and use of a continuously indexed epi-liminf require an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Quotient–Subderivative Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Interfaces linking difference-quotient convergence to subderivative limits.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and finite at \(\bar x\).
The functions \(\Delta_t f(\bar x)\) epigraphically converge as \(t\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_e f(\bar x)=\operatorname{e\!\!-\!lim}_{t\downarrow0}\Delta_t f(\bar x)=df(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order epi-differentiability identifies quotient limits with the lower subderivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\) when the quotient family has an epigraphical limit as \(t\downarrow0\). In that case its epiderivative is defined by \[d_e f(\bar x):=\operatorname{e\!\!-\!lim}_{t\downarrow0}\Delta_t f(\bar x).\] Because the epigraphical lower limit always has values \(df(\bar x)(w)\), existence of the full epigraphical limit yields, for every \(w\in\mathbb R^d\), \[d_e f(\bar x)(w)=df(\bar x)(w).\] Hence epi-differentiability is precisely the condition under which the quotient-to-subderivative correspondence is realized by a genuine epigraphical limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the first-order quotient family epi-converges, its epigraphical limit is the lower subderivative and is called the epiderivative.
knowledge_statements.title: Quotient–Subderivative Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits Quotient–Subderivative Correspondence, but the exact definition of epi-differentiability, any properness requirements on the epiderivative, and the asserted identification with the lower subderivative depend on source conventions. A specific authoritative locator is required.

children.title: Subgradient Limit Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Variational-limit behavior of subgradient mappings.

assumptions_latex: \(f_n,f:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions and \(f_n\xrightarrow{e}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\in\partial f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex outer-limit interface with function-value convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(n\), the inclusion \(v_n\in\partial f_n(x_n)\) means \[f_n(y)\ge f_n(x_n)+\langle v_n,y-x_n\rangle\qquad\text{for every }y\in\mathbb R^d.\] Under epigraphical convergence, convergence of the base points, subgradients, and attained function values passes this inequality to the limit along recovery sequences. The limiting inequality is \[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle v,y-x\rangle\qquad\text{for every }y\in\mathbb R^d,\] which is equivalent to \(v\in\partial f(x)\). Thus value-attentive graphical outer limits of convex subgradients remain subgradients of the epigraphical limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex epi-convergent functions, convergent subgradients remain subgradients of the limit when the associated points and function values also converge.
knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient Limit Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional convex outer-limit theorem is mathematically plausible and theorem is the correct role for Subgradient Limit Interfaces. The statement contains proof text, and no source is supplied for the precise hypotheses, especially the necessity and formulation of function-value convergence. A theorem-level authoritative citation is required.

children.title: Normal-Cone Limit Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Set-limit behavior of normal-cone mappings.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two sequential interface conditions are equivalent to \(\operatorname{gph}N_{C_n}\to\operatorname{gph}N_C\) in the Painlevé--Kuratowski sense.

notation.meaning: Painlevé--Kuratowski outer and inner set limits.
Limiting normal cone to a closed set.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: sequential characterization of graphical convergence for set-valued normal-cone mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential finite-dimensional interface for limiting normal cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A normal-cone limit interface from \(C_n\) to \(C\) holds when both of the following conditions are satisfied. First, whenever \(x_{n_k}\to x\), \(v_{n_k}\to v\), and \(v_{n_k}\in N_{C_{n_k}}(x_{n_k})\), one has \(v\in N_C(x)\). Second, for every \((x,v)\in\operatorname{gph}N_C\), there exist \(x_n\to x\) and \(v_n\to v\) with \(v_n\in N_{C_n}(x_n)\). Equivalently,
\[\operatorname*{Limsup}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{gph}N_{C_n}\subset\operatorname{gph}N_C\subset\operatorname*{Liminf}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{gph}N_{C_n}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normal cones converge graphically exactly when all convergent normal pairs have valid limits and every limiting normal pair can be approximated.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Limit Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sequential outer and inner conditions correctly express Painleve--Kuratowski graphical convergence of the limiting normal-cone mappings, and the content kind fits the interface leaf. No inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied, so the record remains source-dependent.

children.title: Indicator–Normal Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Transfer between indicator-function limits and normal-cone limits.

assumptions_latex: Subdifferentials and normal cones are taken in the same limiting sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\), \(\partial\delta_C(x)=N_C(x)\).

notation.meaning: Limiting subdifferential and limiting normal cone.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limiting construction; for convex sets it specializes to convex subgradients and convex normals.

source_refs.locator: 2.5.2 Specific Normal and Subdifferential Structures p. 235
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the indicator of \(C\) by \(\delta_C(x)=0\) for \(x\in C\) and \(\delta_C(x)=+\infty\) for \(x\notin C\). Then
\[\partial\delta_C(x)=N_C(x)\qquad(x\in\mathbb{R}^d).\]
In particular, both sides are empty when \(x\notin C\). If \(C\) is convex, the common set at \(x\in C\) is
\[\{v\in\mathbb{R}^d:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le 0\ \text{for every }y\in C\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of a closed set's indicator function is exactly the set's normal cone, with matching limiting or convex conventions.
knowledge_statements.title: Indicator–Normal Correspondence

source_witnesses.locator: 2.5.2 Specific Normal and Subdifferential Structures p. 235
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\(v\in\partial f(x)\), and the second epi-derivative at \((x,v)\) exists as a proper function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The subgradient graphical derivative satisfies \(D(\partial f)(x\mid v)=\partial(\tfrac12 d_e^2f(x\mid v))\).

notation.meaning: Second epi-derivative of the function at the primal-dual pair.
Graphical derivative of the subdifferential mapping.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex second-order epi-differentiability interface.

source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I
Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(t>0\), define
\[q_t(w)=\frac{f(x+tw)-f(x)-t\langle v,w\rangle}{\tfrac12t^2}.\]
If \(q_t\) epi-converges as \(t\downarrow0\) to the proper second epi-derivative \(d_e^2f(x\mid v)\), then the tangent limit of subgradient graphs is represented by
\[D(\partial f)(x\mid v)(w)=\partial\!\left(\tfrac12 d_e^2f(x\mid v)\right)(w).\]
Thus second-order difference-quotient limits identify the first graphical variation of the subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a twice epi-differentiable convex function, the graphical derivative of its subdifferential is the subdifferential of half its second epi-derivative.
knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Variational Limit Interfaces

source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I
Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I
